utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, Tuesday, the 9th of March, 2010, I would like to greet everyone present, the accused, the Defence teams, Mr. Scott and his assistants, and everyone else assisting us. Mr. Scott, I believe there is something you would like to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. If I could have the assistance of the usher, please, for the ELMO. Thanks very much. Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President, each of Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, perhaps it comes as no surprise, or perhaps it does, but I hope the Chamber has observed that we have moved -- or I have attempted to move as quickly as possible, covering some fairly complex issues. I have spent days repeatedly cutting our material, including late into the evening last night, to what I consider, with all respect, essentially bare-bones. I've put on the ELMO a number of topics that I would still hope to address, at least briefly. You'll see Prozor 1992, January of 1993, April of 1993, Mostar -- matters related to Mostar on the 8th and 10th of May, 1993, camps and detention, forced labour, and, finally, HVO crimes and responsibility. Even, Your Honour -- I will say that even with additional time, it will be hard -- frankly, we'll be hard-pressed, and we'll have to take these matters ever so briefly. But I am asking Your Honour, in light of everything we've done -- I've tried to be patient, as much as possible, with Mr. Petkovic and not cut him off any more than I felt like I had to. But, in any event, Your Honour, for all these reasons the Prosecution would ask to have one additional hour to complete its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. The Petkovic objects to this request for a simple reason: If you have a look at the amount of time Mr. Scott has used to deal with the issue of credibility, to deal with the issue of the presidential transcript dated the 13th of April, 1999, which is P8912, if we see how much time he spent on certain parts of General Petkovic's testimony on the Kordic and Blaskic cases, if we have a look at the amount of time he repeated his questions, we'll come to the simple conclusion that at least an hour and a half too much has been spent on that subject, or in the course of that hour and a half not a single new answer of substance was provided. If my colleague Mr. Scott had used his time in a more rational way, he wouldn't need additional time now. This is why we firmly object to this request and believe that it would not be fair to allocate the Prosecution more additional time, which would mean that he would have, roughly speaking, 60 per cent more time for his cross-examination than the Defence had for its examination-in-chief. All these subjects that have been listed here, had they been prepared in an appropriate way -- or if they'd been prepared in an appropriate way, that would make it possible to examine General Petkovic quite briefly. But if one continues repeating questions, then in the next three hours we'll have a new request for additional time from my colleague Mr. Scott. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I can respond briefly. If the Prosecution, and more specifically myself, is being accused of having not conducted a perfect cross-examination, then I plead guilty. I don't think there is such a thing as a perfect examination by any party. We've certainly tried. I think the Chamber can see, over the last several days, what the Prosecution has attempted to do. Has, sometimes, maybe has one topic gone on longer than ideally it might have? Perhaps. Again, no one is perfect. I think the Chamber has watched the answers and responses of Mr. Petkovic. The Prosecution respectfully submits that over and over again he has been non-responsive. If you get direct answers, responsive answers, to a question the first time, you don't have to keep asking the same question over and over again, you don't have to intervene, you don't have to keep going back, and that's what the Prosecution has had to deal with. At the end of the day, Your Honours, even if the Chamber were to give the Prosecution another hour, the Prosecution still would have had substantially less -- substantially less time than all the examinations that preceded the Prosecution taking the floor, substantially less. Your Honours, you've seen -- I've put the matters up for you specifically so you could see that not just speaking in abstract the topics to be covered, and to attempt to do those, and with the additional hour, Your Honours, I think we have some prospect, but even that will be tight. But I dare not ask the Chamber for more time than I have, and I would be grateful -- I would be most grateful to the Chamber to allow us this additional time to continue to assist the Chamber, I hope, as much as we can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I'd like to respond. The claim made by my colleague Mr. Karnavas, according to which Mr. Petkovic didn't provide direct and brief answers to the questions put, let's briefly remember the sort of questions Mr. Scott put. The questions contained several factual allegations, and then he wanted an answer, a yes-or-no answer. Such answers can't be provided to such questions. If Mr. Scott had put questions to which a yes-or-no answer could be provided, at least a yes-or-no answer for each particular segment of the question, then General Petkovic would have certainly answered the questions in that way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has taken note of the Prosecution's request for additional time, and on the basis of the chart we have noted that an entire series of subjects could be invoked with this additional time. The Chamber has also taken note of the Defence position, which objects to additional time, because according to the Defence, the Prosecution should have used its time more proficiently when putting questions. In addition, the Chamber notes that on a number of occasions the witness did not answer the questions in a precise manner, which meant that the Prosecution had to use up more time than initially planned. Having put everything in the balance, the Chamber is of the opinion that it would be in the interests of justice for the Prosecution to be allowed to put questions that concern the subjects on the Prosecution list, and as a result the Chamber hereby allocates the Prosecution an additional 45 minutes. Mr. Scott, so you had two hours and five minutes left, plus forty-five minutes, which amounts to a total of two hours and fifty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm most grateful to the Chamber, and I trust I'll try to use the time wisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is there anything the Petkovic Defence would like to say? If not, we will call General Petkovic into court.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really have nothing I would like to add. To discuss the possibility of filing an appeal would be senseless, so I think it would be best to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I greet you on behalf of my colleagues and in person. The Prosecution has asked for additional time, and the Chamber has granted the Prosecution 45 additional minutes. I wanted to inform you of this fact. I would also like to remind you that the Prosecution is putting very precise questions to you. You can answer them by saying, Yes, or, No, or, I don't know. And if the Prosecution wants additional information, you may then provide the Prosecution with your overall vision of the events. But for the moment, I'd like to remind you of the fact that you are in the hands of the Prosecution, and the Prosecution can conduct its cross-examination as it deems fit. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, once again, good morning to all those in and around the courtroom, with our thanks for your assistance, especially the patience of the interpreters, I must say. And good morning to you, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, we were ending the day, and I hope to finish the topic of Stupni Do very quickly. That's my goal, at least. But we left on the topic -- we were talking about your knowledge and the knowledge of the HVO of the reputation for bad conduct that a number of the units, in particular in the Kiseljak area, had, including the Maturice and the Apostoli that the Prosecution puts, at least, were the units involved in Vares and substantially involved in Vares and Stupni Do at the end of October 1993. You indicated at the very end of the day that -- you said: "Your Honour, not a single report on the behaviour of the Maturice, in the sense the Prosecutor is saying, exist." And I'd like you, sir, to begin by turning, please, to -- it would be in the same binder we were using yesterday, I believe, P11196. It's in the set of -- if I'm not mistaken, it's in the set of the two -- binder 2, but the set of two binders, a two-binder set, and in the second binder toward the end, sir. P11196. Sir, this is a report to Mr. Blaskic and others, Mr. Sliskovic, dated the 11th of August, 1993. And, again, we don't have time to cover as many documents as one might like, but at the bottom of the -- I'm not sure where it will be in the Croatian -- the end of the document, essentially, so I think it's fairly easy to find, the very bottom of the document, last paragraph: "In the evening of 9 August 1993, a group of Maturice JPN members seriously breached rules of military conduct; namely, in the village called Drazevici on the Kiseljak-Sarajevo highway. They stopped several vehicles and just stood on the road drinking alcohol. This was followed by verbal duals and shooting from automatic weapons in the air. According to some information, several hand-grenades were thrown at a nearby Muslim house where Croatian refugees were put up, was torched." Now, I grant it, that may not be exactly the scope of the conduct that was committed, according to the Prosecution's case, in Stupni Do; but that is, indeed, one example of a report of misconduct by the Maturice, isn't it? And that can be answered, Yes, or, No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is an internal clash between their members, nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer is, Yes. If you can please turn to P1080 -- excuse me, P10809 in the same binder, also, I believe, toward the back. This was an interview given by Mr. Bandic, the same Mr. Bandic who testified in this case, the same Mr. Bandic who was involved in a number of intelligence operations, including here in The Hague. And when Mr. Bandic was interviewed by, I believe, it's "Globus" -- and I should pause and say this is the same Mr. Bandic that you told us you were particularly close to. You testified on direct examination about

utterances.speaker: MR. BANDIC AT 49626
utterances.text: "We worked in the same room and we slept under the same roof, so all the information that I had access to was also available to Mr. Bandic." And in similar fashion, sir, I put to you, based on this relationship and the roles played, all the information that Mr. Bandic had was also available to you. And if you look at Exhibit P10809, on page 9 of the translation, it's a section, sir: "The decapitator of Kiseljak. Como brought in a dozen cut-off heads of Bosniak soldiers." Bandic is asked: "Who are Rajic's most trusted men, those that he now shifts the on to. Dominko Ilijasevic, Como, and Miroslav Anic, aka Firga, those were real sadists and men with real criminal records. I remember that Como brought to Kiseljak a dozen Bosniak heads after some military action and left them near a wall on the main cross roads in full view of everybody. They did not escape the attention of the representatives in the international community either." That information was widely publicised and widely known and known to you, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bandic verified this information; UNPROFOR, too. This information wasn't correct. Mr. Bandic didn't discover a single case that had occurred. He received information and publicised it, but it hadn't been verified. Members of UNPROFOR discussed the matter for two days, and they said that they didn't see anything. You should ask General Filijala and General Prada. I spoke to them with respect to this subject. Mr. Bandic didn't find a single piece of information. He accepted someone's story, but he didn't go into the details, he didn't verify this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that it was, in fact, widely reported at the time and widely known at the time, and you know that full well. I would like you to turn, please, to P09818, P09818, in the same binder. This is an order you sent to Mr. Rajic on the 6th of November, 1993. Sir, I just want to quickly point out a couple of things. This is an order that you sent: "1. Units from Kiseljak should urgently retreat from the area of Vares ..." Item 5: "Do not waste time on attempting to regain the control of Vares. Direct your efforts at executing the planned task in Kiseljak." And I put it to you, sir, and continuing with the theme that we were talking about yesterday, the reason that you told Mr. Rajic, Forget about Vares, is because there was no intent and there never was any intention by the HVO at this point in time to try to keep Vares. And you made that point very clear twice in this order, sir, Don't worry about Vares, don't go back there, don't worry about it, move on with the other -- with the plan. And that's the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vares fell. I wanted these units to be withdrawn, the ones that arrived from Kiseljak, nothing else. And other HVO units remained in the Dastansko settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go back now to P10809, the interview with Mr. Bandic that we were looking about -- excuse me, looking at a few moments ago, P10809, page 8 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, a moment ago the Prosecution showed a document to you, P10809. It's an interview Mr. Bandic gave for "Globus" on the 2nd of December, 2005. There's a lot of information in the interview. We don't have time to go into everything, but there is something that drew my attention. The journalist asked him about the KOS, and in particular about Tuta belonging to the KOS and in particular about Tuta belonging to the KOS. And Bandic says that in his opinion, Tuta wasn't a KOS member, but at the end of the sentence something is added. He says that there was serious indicia -- significant indicia according to which Rajic was a KOS collaborator under the name of Bojan Radic. So what would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such information arrived from Mr. Bandic, and Mr. Bandic, even before the war, worked in Security Services of Yugoslavia. He didn't start doing that in the war. He was a security officer or official before the war, too. As for the information he had about Rajic, I don't know whether this is correct or not, but there was no official information that arrived in the Main Staff or anywhere else about Rajic, about the fact that Rajic was apparently a KOS employee. This is the first time he mentioned this in his interview, that Rajic was a KOS collaborator. All the SIS documents that the Main Staff had access to didn't mention that Rajic was a KOS collaborator. I read this in this interview for the first time, the allegation that Rajic was a KOS collaborator. And before the war, as I said, Mr. Bandic worked in the Security Services of the former state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you know nothing about that. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the same document, sir, if we could turn to the -- I was saying on page 8 of the English translation, you will find a box, if you will, or part of the text which is titled "Saving a War Criminal": "Susak ordered that Rajic be hidden in Croatia. Why did Rajic change his name to Viktor Andric? "That was Boban's order." Next question: "Did General Petkovic know of the change of Rajic's identity? "Yes, he conveyed the order to him. "How was Rajic taken away from BiH anyway? "A refuge was found for him in Croatia by an order of Minister Gojko Susak. They found him a job, and as I learned later, a false identity was created for him. "Did General Petkovic know that? "He did." All that is true, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have seen, when Rajic changed his name, he sent information to the Main Staff and to myself, saying that he had changed his name. That's all I knew about the change of name. As to how he changed his name and why, I don't know. Here we have seen a document, and it says that Rajic informed this change of name to Viktor Andric. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You know that full well, sir. You were part and parcel of that entire course of events, the whole facade, the whole subterfuge of Viktor Andric. You and Mr. Rajic communicated back and forth together, using that name, and telling you that he had changed his name. That's well known to you, sir, and I put to you what Mr. Bandic says here, in this instance, at least, these four points, are entirely accurate and true, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know he had changed his name. He sent information according to which he was changing his name. As to how this was done and why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a significant difference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've said several times that the HVO was not preparing for war with the Muslims, but I put it to you, sir, that, in fact, at least by the second half of 1992, they were, indeed, preparing for war with the Muslims. You claim, sir -- you appear to claim that the war with the Muslims began in Konjic in March or April of 1993, and I put it to you, sir, quite the contrary. The war began in September/October 1992 in Prozor and Novi Travnik; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't a war. There was situations in which there were incidents - that's what we called them - and in two or three days' time we gained control over the situation and these incidents no longer broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, one man's incidents is another man's war, I suppose. It didn't all happen and escalate overnight, but I put it to you, and you know full well, that it was the views of the Croat leadership, both in Herceg-Bosna and in Croatia, that war with the Muslims was inevitable in the second half of 1992 and preparations and steps were being taken to prepare for exactly that war; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Sanction slide 32, please. It will be on the screen, and I'll read it slowly, sir, parts of it to put to you, if you listen to translation. Sir, some presidential transcripts, P00353, 1 August 1992, page 30: "Tudjman: I know, but nevertheless, it has to be decided, if there is no Croatian population over there, you cannot wage war in another territory without declaring war. Who are you going to declare war to? Izetbegovic has hardly agreed to that wording in the agreement." And if I pause there, sir, far from having reached any sort of agreement about this in July of 1992 or otherwise, you and the HVO and the Croat leadership knew, in fact, that Mr. Izetbegovic and the BiH government had not actually reached any agreement about Herceg-Bosna or the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to ask Mr. Scott to tell us what binder that's in so that we can follow the document ourselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Binder number 1 of the second set, P00353.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, and my question is pending to you. You knew -- and I'll just read it to you again. Far from having reached any sort of agreement about this --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to have a look at the whole document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While you're doing that, sir, I'm going to put my question to you again, since we were interrupted. Far from having reached any sort of agreement about this in July of 1992 or otherwise, you and the HVO and the Croat leadership knew, in fact, that Mr. Izetbegovic and the BiH government had not actually reached any agreement about Herceg-Bosna or the HVO; isn't that true? Isn't that true, sir? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what agreement Mr. Izetbegovic had agreed to or not, because Herceg-Bosna was a political section, not a military section, and I know what existed in the military section of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P00466 in the same binder, 11 September 1992, page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness asked to be able to look at the document himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not going to look at excerpts before I can see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're looking for the document, Your Honours, the document Mr. Scott showed, P353, the presidential transcripts, an excerpt was read out there without us knowing at all what part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that refers to and whether it refers to Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. And I think that's an important point, because it's important to understand that for us to be able to understand what this excerpt that was quoted refers to at all. So as has been said many times, we have to know the context in which a statement was made for us to be able to comment on the statement, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's well established, after four years, that we don't have time and we never have read long passages of transcripts. There's certainly not time for that. The Chamber has -- the Chamber and the counsel have the page references and the full transcript. I'm sure that if I misrepresent something, that Ms. Alaburic or someone will correct me. I read it accurately, that's what I put to the witness. I'm putting the Prosecution case to the witness, and that's what I put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention, sir, to P00466. On 11 September 1992, Praljak says: "And war with the Muslims can be anticipated. "Susak: We have been aware of that for over a week now, and we made preparations on what needs to be done." And I note that that's just a few weeks before Prozor at the end of October 1992. P00498 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do have to react at this point. Take a look at the whole page in the Croatian, at least. It is quite clear that it refers to Posavina, just like document P353. So both these documents refer to the territory of Posavina. Now, Mr. Scott has the transcript in front of him, and we can see what part is being discussed in the three lines above that, so let's be precise. There's no reason to manipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No one's manipulating, Your Honour. I'm confident that the entire context of the conversation is much -- is broader than what Ms. Alaburic has indicated. It's talking about war with the Muslims, and that's the topic, and Mr. Praljak, of course, knew exactly what he was talking about at the time. P00498, 17 September 1992, at page 29. Mr. Prlic, it says, in a meeting with Mr. Tudjman: "There is still no political agreement regarding the relations between the Croats and the Muslims. These relations are becoming ever more tense, and certain conflicts are looming. Personally, I think it will be impossible to avoid conflicts entirely." 17th of September, 1992. P00524, 26 September 1992. I'm going to go down about halfway through the article: "Tudjman: We are concerned about their wishes to take over the control even in those areas, Croatian areas, that the HVO has liberated and where it has control. "Susak --" that's at page 6: "Susak: They have about 20.000 refugees in Mostar, and orders come from Sarajevo, and now Muslim brigades are being formed in Mostar, Capljina, in Stolac, now that Mostar, Capljina and Stolac have been liberated. We will not allow that." Page 18: "Tudjman: We will openly tell Izetbegovic when he comes here what we said in the beginning. There can be no discussion about them establishing military and civilian government in areas that used to be within the Croatian Banovina." Sir, you know that was the state of -- that was the state of play in August and September 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In this territory, there was no conflict; quite the contrary. This was the time when the Muslims were joining the ranks of the HVO. So I don't know where these stories originated from and who put them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not what Mr. Susak says. One of the things Mr. Susak is complaining about is that the Muslims are now forming and joining Muslim brigades in Mostar, Capljina and Stolac, and Susak says, We will not allow that. That doesn't seem like agreement or census to me, does it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. First of all, the General said that Muslims are joining the HVO, and that's a fact. Now, look at the question, look at the answer, look at the following-up question. This is outrageous. This is not how cross-examination should be done. I don't know what this is. This is a montage where the Prosecution reads, he cherry-picks whatever he feels like. It looks like a closing argument. The Bench is very passive, and I'm rather shocked. I am rather shocked at this technique, after giving the gentleman an hour to conduct cross-examination. This is not cross-examination the likes I've ever seen in any court anywhere around the world. This is improper. This is closing argument by using the witness. Look at the question, look at the answer, look at the following question. There's a disconnect there. And I think if Mr. Scott wishes to do cross-examination, he should cross-examine. He should put his case, and the gentleman can answer. But this is not a proper way, by taking a montage of various, very complex presidential transcripts, cherry-picking, when nobody has the time to actually look at the context in which everything was said. And we're all sitting here passive, waiting for the slaughter. I think this is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when the Prosecutor is putting to the witness an extract, a sentence which has been pulled out of context, he has to give the accused -- I beg your pardon, the witness enough time to locate the sentence in the text among those 15 binders that he has, to find the exact sentence, and to find where that discussion begins and ends. And you saw the transcripts yourselves. Very often it's not quite clear what they're talking about. So if the witness is being put a case, Susak says this and that, then, according to logics, you have to provide the witness a few minutes to find the page and to see what Susak says exactly, and what was being discussed in the first place; so that having done that, as a witness, he can provide his opinions about it all, because this is quite unacceptable, an unacceptable technique. And had we done that, I'm sure that the Prosecution would have us up and the Court would have us up for contempt. It's impermissible, regardless of time. If he has the time, let him proceed step by step. If he hasn't, he'll have to do it another way. And, anyway, he's putting his case within the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a remark. Mr. Karnavas is astonished that the Chamber is not intervening. As far as I'm concerned, and I think my colleagues agree with me, we are listening to the questions of the Prosecutor, who, on the basis of his table, is recalling that in the month of September, several people spoke, General Praljak, Mr. Prlic, Tudjman, regarding the question of the conflict which is looming. And Mr. Prlic, himself, announces that there is a risk of a conflict breaking out. P00498. The Prosecutor is showing to General Petkovic what Tudjman, himself, says, saying that he will not accept the formation of an authority, military and civilian, in areas which used to be part of the Croatian Banovina. The Prosecutor is endeavouring, through his questions, to elicit the point of view of General Petkovic on a particular issue, which is the case of the Prosecutor concerning the joint criminal enterprise. And in the interests of justice, it seems to me important for General Petkovic to respond on the basis of the documents in front of him. That is the case of the Prosecutor, and no more and no less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If that's going to be the case, then you have to give the general and the rest of us sufficient time to look at all of these excerpts to see in which context, because I would like to be able to object whenever something is taken out of context. It is impermissible to take one line out of an entire discussion and say, Based on this line from this page and this line from this page, from here we can draw some conclusions. These are complex discussions. The person who's being questioned certainly should have the opportunity to look at in which context something was said. That's my point. And since we don't have enough time, this sort of a technique is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the question that was pending to you some moments ago before the interruptions were: You had said you didn't know where these stories came from or originated from, and put on page 17 of today's transcript. I then put to you that's not what Mr. Susak says. One of the things Mr. Susak is complaining about is the Muslims are now forming and joining Muslim brigades in Mostar, Capljina and Stolac, and Susak says, We will not allow that. That doesn't seem like agreement or consensus to me, does it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, Your Honours, that this was a time when most Muslims -- when a lot of Muslims were joining the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Brigades of the HVO in the Mostar area. This was also a time when you saw that the Bregava Brigade, for example, was offering to come under the command of the 1st Brigade so that they could carry out their assignments jointly. This was also a time when, together with the BH Army, we were planning and carrying out the joint operation in November. This was a time when a joint operative command for defence was issued, active defence, for the whole Neretva River Valley. So I don't know how come Susak and the others are discussing the situation in this way. The situation on the ground was not like that. This was a time when at least 2 to 3.000 Muslims had already joined the Croatian Defence Council and were defending positions around Mostar together with us, Mostar, Stolac and Capljina, and were taking part later on in operations against the Serbs, so this -- there are no arguments to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, our time is limited. I think you've given your answer, as opposed to the credit of the Muslims, that they so actively participated so long in the HVO. But let me ask you to turn to P00479, P00479. That will be in the same binder, just one or two documents previous to the one we were looking at just a moment ago, P00479. With these statements that I put to you in mind, sir, this is an agenda prepared by the head of the Croatian Army, Mr. Bobetko, on the 15th of September, 1992. Mr. Bobetko says, among other things: "In order to improve operative-tactical situation on the Herzegovina front and determine the actual task, I hereby establish the following:" An agenda. Item 1.1: "Estimation of possibilities for attacks along the direction and manner of securing the taken positions." This is apparently assigned to you: "Organised by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic." 2.1: "The estimation of operative-tactical situation along the directions in winter conditions of warfare to be organised by Mr. Siljeg." Item number 3: "Basic characteristics of commanding. Authorities on Herzegovina front." Presented by the commander of the front, and I note this October -- excuse me, September of 1992: "Presented by the commander of the front, Croatian Army General Bobetko. "Because of the important of the agenda, the following civil and military organs are due to attend the meeting." And let's just go down the list quickly: Milivoj Petkovic, Ante Jelavic, heavily involved in HVO logistics, as the Chamber has heard about, Mr. Obradovic, Mr. Lasic, Mr. Akrap. Mr. Akrap was another officer who was HV; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an HV officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Siljeg, chief of the Military Police Administration, Mr. Coric; civilian structure, head of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic; HZ-HB Prime Minister Jadranko Prlic. Virtually, sir, with a couple of exceptions, the entire cast of characters, I put to you. And then Mr. Bobetko says: "I will personally do my best so that Susak and Boban also attend the meeting." So I put to you, sir, by all indications, this was a hugely important planning meeting for the HVO about four weeks before the events in Prozor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, you're not right. This deals with the southern part below Mostar. And after that, Operation Bura was being prepared, and that coincides with the time when the Yugoslav Army was supposed to leave the soil of the Republic of Croatia. So this has nothing to do with Prozor, and don't push it into that bracket. Operation Bura came out of this, and these were the first preparations to move towards Nevesinje or, rather, Trebinje. And Nevesinje and Trebinje are below Mostar to the south, and we have heard about that operation, and these are the first intimations of it and an agreement that such an operation was being prepared to push back the Serbs as far from the Neretva River and Valley as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to January of 1993, sir, in the interests of time. Could I ask you to look at slide -- Sanction slide number 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think there is a problem in the transcript. On page 24, line 1, the end of Mr. Petkovic's answer, I heard in original language he said, "And that has nothing to do with events in Prozor." This crucial sentence, which closes his entire response, is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I said that that has nothing to do with Prozor. After that, preparations were underway and Operation Bura was underway and the attempt to break through to Nevesinje and further into Eastern Herzegovina which was held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the assistance of the usher, please, for the ELMO. Apparently these are not available in Sanction. I'm sure it was probably my fault. If you could put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, turning briefly to January of 1993 and the events during that time, you testified under oath in the Blaskic case at 24215 to 16: "Yes, I wish to say that the Vance-Owen Plan was presented to us in January 1993 and that it was not accepted by all three parties, so I never talked to Blaskic about the Vance-Owen Plan, nor did I ever discuss it with him. After all, it had not been accepted either, so I think there is no point in discussing a plan that was not accepted." And if we can similarly turn to what would be, I just say for the record, slide 56, but we're putting it on the ELMO, you gave similar testimony some months later in the Kordic case at page 26727 to 28: "Your Honours, the Vance-Owen Plan to be referred to in this January 1993 period is not logical, because all three parties had not signed it. We cannot talk about it in January 1993. It's not a plan, it's a draft plan signed by only one party. It becomes a plan when all three parties sign it. So I didn't pay any attention --" excuse me. "I didn't pay attention to the Vance-Owen Plan. We waited and hoped that it would be signed. There was a plan, but it hadn't been signed, so it is not an official document until it is signed for us or for them, though we did all do our best to have it signed so that the conflicts would end." Now, you stand by your testimony in both the Blaskic case and the Kordic case on that point, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's common knowledge that all three sides did not sign the plan and that the plan fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn next in the exhibits to P01344 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, this document prompts me to ask you a question which I have been thinking over throughout the weekend, after seeing the video showing the formation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And we see that there was a meeting with more than 60 people who declare the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. We saw last week that you were present, and I even asked you whether you had voted, and you said, no, you hadn't voted. According to the video and according to the transcript of the video, this meeting lasted quite a long time, and the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna appears to have been the logical follow-up of the Vance-Owen Plan because several participants intervened and mentioned the issue. And now I see this page 26727 from the Kordic testimony, in which you appear to say that since the plan was not signed by all the parties, the conclusion could perhaps be drawn that there was no interest in this plan; maybe, I don't know. But how would you reconcile your statement which we have here in front of us with the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which seems to have been the fruit of the Vance-Owen Plan? How can you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't the fruit of the Vance-Owen Plan. In June, the Serbs refused to sign the Vance-Owen Plan. I think it was on the 6th of June, in actual fact, when the Assembly of the Republika Srpska rejected Karadzic's signature in Athens, thereby making the Vance-Owen Plan null and void. And another plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan appeared, and a union of the three republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina [Realtime transcript read in error "Herceg-Bosna"] was mentioned there, and on the basis of that, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed. And, on the other hand, there was the provisional formation of the Republic of Bosna which was done by the Muslim representatives. They held that for several days. I don't know why they gave up on that. So Herceg-Bosna came into being as an agreement on a union made up of three republics, so that was the new plan when the Vance-Owen Plan fell through. A new plan was created, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, as it was called, which speaks of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the union of three republics. And it's interesting to note that at that same time in Sarajevo, the Republic of Bosna was proclaimed as well. That was what it was called. And that's what happened at that time in Grude, when the political representatives of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, led by this plan, proclaimed the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction to the transcript. On page 26, line 18, it says "Herceg-Bosna," and it should say "Bosnia-Herzegovina," because the general spoke about that and said that according to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, three republics should be formed in Bosnia and Herzegovina; one Serb, one Muslim, and one Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what the plan was, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer, but you said something that I discovered just now. You said in Sarajevo - this is line 2, page 27 - the Republic of Bosna was proclaimed. If my understanding is correct, that means that Mr. Izetbegovic makes a follow-up to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan by declaring the Republic of Bosna, without mentioning Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Muslim side, at the time the Republic of Bosna was proclaimed, but I don't know after how much time this agreement that they reached they annulled that act. And you were able to see that, I think, through a Prlic witness who spoke about that in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: Were you aware of the Cutileiro Plan and of the Lisbon Declaration? In fact, there was three. Did you follow all this closely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did know about the Cutileiro Plan, and he spoke about three constituent peoples and three constituent units, and it was a condition for people to go to a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to build up a Bosnia-Herzegovina of that kind, with the three constituent peoples and three constituent units. And Mr. Izetbegovic, when he -- when Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed independent, he gave up on the idea and did not want to refer to what Cutileiro's plan offered anymore, and it was a condition for the referendum. And if the referendum was successful, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be proclaimed independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your answers show that you are familiar with the subject. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, indeed, sir. Based on that familiarity, you will also recall that Mr. Karnavas played you a video, an interview with Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Prlic at that point said -- was discussing the negotiations and peace plans, and Mr. Prlic said to the effect, Talk is talk, negotiations are negotiations, there's no agreement until there is an agreement, and, in fact, until it actually, after some time, amounts to something. And Mr. Karnavas asked if you agreed with Mr. Prlic's assessment, and you said that you did, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a complete agreement is when all three sides have signed it, but all three sides did not sign it. But it's another matter that the Muslim representatives -- or, rather, the Bosniak representatives changed their minds after a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, sir, that may be the case, and we don't have to debate that. But assuming for the moment that's the case, that's the nature of negotiations, isn't it? There's no deal until there is a deal. And it may be frustrating to one party or another, but until there is a final agreement, there is no agreement, and you know full well that that was frequently the case. And one of the interviewed you gave back at the time, I believe it was in January of 1994, perhaps, you talked about that. And you said there were so many cease-fires and so many agreements that over time they were essentially worthless. And I think you said something to the effect of, I would wait to at least five days after any cease-fire was signed to see if it actually amounted to anything. Do you remember saying things like that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say something to that effect. But this agreement on three republics started off, and we don't know why the Bosniak side stopped short.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, I think we could discuss that and I could help you with that, but we don't have time to go into the details. The bottom line, sir, is just like Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg was never agreed, it was never a plan. It was just like everything else, as Mr. Prlic said, Talk is talk, negotiations are negotiations. Owen-Stoltenberg was never signed, and there was no agreement until finally the Washington Agreement at the end of February 1994, or March; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were indications and instructions that we should start working on it, and no one called in question Bosnia-Herzegovina by so doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's turn, please, to P01344, which we started to go to, I think, some moments ago, P01344. This is an order from you, dated the 29th of January, 1993, and I want to direct your attention, in particular, to item number 3, an order to Mr. Siljeg: "3. Point out to the other side that you have given instructions for a list to be made of Muslim refugees from Gornji Vakuf municipality in the Republic of Croatia and that we will return them to Vakuf as soon as possible. Quote this as my order and really do charge someone from the civilian structure with obtaining a list." And then if we go to -- keep that in mind, and one might want to keep a finger on that, and turn to P01354, which is the very next document, so it should be fairly easy, P01354. Mr. Siljeg responds on the same day, or implements -- goes forward on the same day, 29 January 1993, to HVO Gornji Vakuf. The president: "Instructions for further work. Urgently try to draw up a list of Muslims from Vakuf who are in the Republic of Croatia as refugees. "We need this in order to so inform the Muslim delegation in our negotiations with them and to threaten them that they will be returned to Gornji Vakuf." Sir, you and Mr. Siljeg agreed on a plan -- a more -- more accurately. You order that a course of action to threaten the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, that if they didn't do what you wanted them to do, steps would be taken to round up any Muslim refugees that were then in the Republic of Croatia and send them back to Gornji Vakuf; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that. They said that the refugees had left because of the fighting, and we said we'd make a list to see when each person had left Gornji Vakuf, that it wasn't due to the fighting, but that there were people who had fled in 1992 and before that, ever since June onwards. Nobody had threatened them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Siljeg makes it very clear. Mr. Siljeg makes it very clear ... [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Scott, just a second, please. I think it will be useful for all of us for the General to tell us -- "They said." Tell us, General, who were "they" so we know who we're talking about. Who wanted this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Representatives of the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not for counsel to put questions during my cross-examination. Pardon me. If she wants to come back in redirect, she can. I'm conducting the examination at this point, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's quite clear -- Mr. Siljeg is quite clear, sir, in response to your order to threaten them, "threaten them, they will be returned to Gornji Vakuf," that's what it says, and that is what you intended, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the gist of what I had said. They had tried to accuse us that the war and the conflict in Gornji Vakuf -- that is, the Muslim representatives at the negotiations claimed that this was due to the fact that a certain number of people had fled to Croatia, and I said we'd make a list to see how many had left and when they had gone to Croatia, starting from 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's turn to Exhibit P01092, P01092 in the same binder. Also in January 1993, sir, this is a communication from the same Mr. Siljeg, dated the 10th of January, 1993. Mr. Siljeg says, in the first paragraph: "In recent days we have been confronted with a larger number of requests by persons of Muslim nationality from Livno to leave the HVO and join the Army of BiH ..." Going to the second paragraph: "Proposal: to allow the departure from HZ-HB territories, but not outside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, accompanied by previous returning of weaponry and equipment which was issued to them by the HVO, and take their families with them -- take their families with them and not to return afterwards." In other words, leave Herceg-Bosna, take your families with you, and don't come back. And you responded to Mr. Siljeg in Exhibit P11212, in the second -- it's the second binder, Your Honour. I guess it's in a different binder from what we were just using. P11212. On the 14th of January, sir, 1993, you respond to Mr. Siljeg's proposal, and you say: "I agree with your suggestion, and you should state it as bluntly as possible." You endorsed the plan, Tell the Muslims, yes, they can leave the HVO if they wish, as long as they take their families, leave Herceg-Bosna, and don't come back; that's what you agreed -- that's what you endorsed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're interpreting this quite wrongly. If you wish, I can explain. Neither did the Muslims leave Livno, nor did they go anyway. There was no ABiH army in Livno. The closest ABiH was 50 kilometres from Livno. The SDA is blackmailing the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't matter if it was 50 kilometres away, and you're not answering the question. You're doing -- you're misdirecting. The question had nothing to do with where the local HVO unit was located. Mr. Siljeg says quite clearly, The Muslims are leaving the HVO and want to join the ABiH. I don't care if they want to join them in Livno, or Tomislavgrad, or Ruda [sic] -- or Grude, or anywhere else. Mr. Siljeg states a proposition, he proposes a course of action to you, and you endorsed it, Yeah, let them go, in fact, tell them very bluntly, do go, take your families with you, get out of Herceg-Bosna, and don't come back. That's what you agreed to, isn't it? Not "agreed." You ordered it.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what the documents indicate, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest that the witness should be given an opportunity to answer. When you see the question, he must be given the opportunity to fully respond, and he was responding to the question. It is another thing that the Prosecutor doesn't like this response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's simply not true, Your Honour. I'm following the same rules that we followed for the last four years, and it's counsel that apparently doesn't like the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Kovacic, I believe that General Petkovic has answered. He said that in Livno, there was no problem. Therefore, he answered. General Petkovic, the document that is being -- the two documents that you are being shown, there is the proposal by Colonel Siljeg and your reply, and these are inculpatory documents. No one can deny that. As they are presented by the Prosecutor, Colonel Siljeg is asking you -- or, rather, proposing to you that Muslims should hand over their weapons and that their families should leave the area. And you -- this seems to be agreeable to you, and you even add that this should be stated to the Muslims in the least courteous possible manner. When one sees these two documents, one could draw the conclusion from them that the departure of Muslim families is satisfactory to you. What is your comment to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are talking about the SDA party from Livno, which tried to blackmail the HVO by saying that the Muslims would leave Livno and join the ABiH. No one prevented them from going, but the closest unit is 50 kilometres away. So Siljeg put the question, Fine, you will go 50 kilometres away, who's going to defend your families, who will you hand over your weapons to, the weapons you received from the HVO? Secondly, You cannot leave the territory of BiH and flee to Croatia. And there were talks between the brigade commander, that is, the Muslims who were in command positions at certain levels in the HVO in Livno municipality, and the actual position was that the Muslims in Livno wanted to form a battalion consisting exclusively of Muslims, and that was the trigger. But the SDA reacted in a different way. It started blackmailing. And Siljeg responded, If that is what you want, if you want to leave Livno, it's a territorial unit, their families are there, their property is there. And when this was made evident to them and when the army soldiers said they didn't want to go anywhere, but that they wanted to have a Muslim battalion, and the problem was resolved within 10 days, and within the Petar Kresimir Brigade all the Muslims who wanted to joined to form a battalion, this battalion was given its own zone of responsibility. It had full logistic support from the brigade. And this battalion, consisting of 350 men, I remember well, with the assistance of the HVO, grew to almost 500 men, and that was the problem. The SDA either didn't have the courage or didn't know how to act and say clearly, Let us have our own battalion in Livno. This was not a problem. In 10 days' time, the brigade commander formed this -- resolved the problem and a Muslim battalion was formed. And it was part of the brigade, it was given its assignment, and the problem was signed. No one left Livno, nor did they go anywhere. That there were fervent discussions and upon the insistence of the SDA and not the Muslim soldiers who were constantly putting pressure to bear on Siljeg and the others. That is how the problem in Livno was resolved. Whether Siljeg acted forcefully, why not? You're going to Jablanica to defend other people's homes. Who's going to defend your homes here? And when the Muslims in the HVA said, We want to have our own battalion, we don't want to go anywhere else, the problem was resolved in 10 days, because that was the time needed for the Muslims to rally from the whole brigade to form their battalion and to go to the north-west of Livno, where there was a front-line. And that is how, in Livno, a battalion consisting exclusively of Muslims who wanted to join were formed. No one left in January, nor later, but the correspondence was very forceful, because the position taken was not a sincere one from the beginning. We want to have our own battalion, and that's it. Once that proposal was made, the problem was resolved in 10 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your reply is very clear. You're saying that the problem was resolved within 10 days, and no Muslim family left Livno because there was a Muslim battalion formed. Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to April of 1993, sir, and I'll ask you to look at Exhibit P01798, P01798. It's a loose document. I am told, Your Honours, that it might, at least in the Judges' binders - I'm not sure about counsel's - it may have been stuck in the front of binder number 3, but it's P01798. The witness might need some assistance, Mr. Usher, yes. Thank you, thank you very much. It's a document the Chamber -- the courtroom has seen a number of times. These are the records -- these are the minutes of a meeting of the HVO HZ-HB on the 3rd of April, 1993. In it, sir, there is discussion of the existence of a joint statement that had been prepared, that Mr. Boban had signed, but Mr. Izetbegovic had not signed. And if you'll orient yourself to the document by finding -- there's a list of six items. Do you see that, sir, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6? Sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to find it and to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you find after -- can you assist us, please, by just telling us, have you found where number 6 is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, below item 6 there is this language: "The HVO HZ-HB hopes that because of the enormous importance of the statement, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic will sign this document because it is yet further evidence of a desire for peace, which everybody wants." Next paragraph: "At this meeting, the HVO HZ-HB adopted the position that if the aforementioned statement is not signed by the leaders of the Muslim delegation in Provinces 3, 8 and 10, then the basic premise of the peace plan, which states that all ethnic armed forces have to withdraw to their domicile provinces should apply, and then following." The next paragraph says, in fact -- stay on it a moment longer: "If the joint statement is not implemented, the appropriate military and other authorities of the HVO HZ-HB shall implement this provision." That's the state of play, sir, at the beginning of April 1993. Now, you've told us, in the course of your testimony, that you didn't know anything about an ultimatum or a decision by the HVO government requesting or requiring that certain -- that the ABiH do certain things by the 15th of April, 1993. That's been your position, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my position is still the same, and I don't see where it says that someone should withdraw from Provinces 3, 8 and 10. You haven't read that out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, the Chamber has the document. We've looked at it, as you know, many times in this courtroom, and I'm sure we'll have time to visit it again. But you said you weren't aware of this and had no involvement in it. I put it to you, sir, that it was widely reported at the time, as it was widely in the regional media. The Chamber has seen a number of media articles before, which we don't have time to go into, but for the record, P01808, P09519, P10675. It was widely reported, sir, that this -- that HVO had issued this decision and that there was a dead-line by the 15th of April. Now, with that in mind, I'd like you next to turn to P1 -- excuse me, P01791.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us see what the obligations are given in this document. There are certain obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will, please, sir, to Exhibit P10791. It's in binder number 2 of the two-binder set -- excuse me, binder 1 -- my apologies. Binder 1 of the two-binder set. There are two. P01791. This is a communication from you, dated the 2nd of April, 1993, the day before the HVO meeting. And you write to Mr. Bozo Rajic, and you say in your reply, item number 1: "The HVO Main Staff accepts the suggestion of a joint meeting, but only after Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic sign a joint statement drafted in Zagreb on 27 March 1993." Number 2: "The signing of a joint statement completely rounds off the preliminary conditions for final and permanent solution for the relations between the HVO and ABiH. "3. Since we are expecting the signing of a joint statement within the next 10 days, our stance is that the meeting should be postponed. "Milivoj Petkovic." Sir, you knew full well what the state of play was, you knew that this was this outstanding matter of a joint statement that Mr. Izetbegovic had not signed and never did sign. And you were completely clued in to events and what was happening at the time and what was about to happen, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I expected the statement to be signed, and that is why I said, We're waiting for the statement to be signed. And then I and Halilovic and Mr. Bozo Rajic would be working on the basis of that statement. I don't say anything else in that document. Therefore, this statement on the 27th of March was discussed in Zagreb between Izetbegovic and Boban, and the Main Staff and the ABiH were waiting what would happen with this joint statement, and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, like everyone else, I've read the document, and I must convey to you the question in my mind. You are writing to the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that the Main Staff will not come to the meeting until the agreement has been signed by Boban and Izetbegovic. And when I see what you wrote, I ask myself a question in relation to what you said. You said that the military is under the authority of the civilian, and through this document we see that, in reality, there is a confusion of roles. You say, I will not come unless it is signed, but isn't it up to Mr. Boban to say, either to Mr. Prlic or to Mr. Stojic, but not to you, who is only the Chief of Staff of the military? Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Bozo Rajic, the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was preparing a meeting between me and Mr. Halilovic. In the meantime, it was reported that a joint statement was being prepared by Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic, and I am informing Mr. Rajic that we should wait for that joint statement which we expected would be signed both by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, and then I and Mr. Halilovic can work on the implementation of that joint statement; nothing more. Therefore, I'm not refusing. I'm communicating with the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Rajic, and I'm asking him to wait until the statement has been signed by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, because we were informed that it was expected that the joint statement would be signed. And then Mr. Rajic and Mr. Halilovic and myself would meet to see what we should do after the signing of the statement. I am not refusing anything. I'm just informing the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you're somebody who is very well informed and who is familiar with a broad scope of subjects very well. You were trained by the JNA, and you are familiar with the chain of command. And I'm astonished, because a defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina wants to organise a meeting which has a political and military significance. At that point, why don't you ask permission from your minister of defence as to the steps to be taken that -- or Mr. Boban, whereas you're taking upon yourself the making of a decision not to participate until the agreement has been signed? That is what is astonishing me with respect to the functioning of the military of the HVO, unless one may believe that your powers were quite considerable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're talking about the defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who is communicating with me and with the Chief of Staff of the ABiH. So Mr. Rajic is the defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he is scheduling a meeting with me and Mr. Halilovic. He's entitled to do this, as defence minister. And I, too, am entitled to communicate with the defence minister of the -- of BH, and he was officially the defence minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I'm informing him that on the 27th of March, a joint statement had been drafted in Zagreb, and that we're expecting it to be signed. And then, in point 2, we will finally settle relationships between the HVO and the ABiH. I didn't know that Mr. Izetbegovic would not sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please ask counsel to wait between the questions and answers. From the introduction, we can see that this is a proposal from the Chief of Staff of the ABiH, and perhaps the preamble explains the level of the communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have answered my question. We're approaching the time for the break, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have one follow-up question to your question, and then I think it would be time for a break and we can move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just on this very point, sir, talking about Mr. -- excuse me, Rajic, you told us repeatedly, and you were quite clear in your testimony so far, the person who you described, in fact, in the Kordic case, as "my minister," "my minister," who was higher than you, who was your superior, who was more powerful than you, you said under oath, in the Kordic case, your minister, defence minister, was Mr. Stojic, and your supreme commander was Mr. Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina the defence minister was Mr. Rajic, and we respected him as defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Bozo Rajic was defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he had greater authority than Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's not -- not in Herceg-Bosna, sir, not in Herceg-Bosna he didn't, and you know that, surely, although we can agree. And it may help to remind the Chamber that, of course, Mr. Bozo Rajic was a Croat, a member of the Bosnia government at that time. Sir, you reported on two instructions from Mr. Stojic and Mr. Boban, as you've told us repeatedly under oath; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic and Mr. Boban were at the HVO level. Bozo Rajic was at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, as such, he issued orders to both me and Halilovic. He even issued an order to Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What we're looking at, sir, now, is not an order. It was a request, a request, in fact, which you declined. You made it very clear, I decline. That's not in response to an order. That's a response to someone's invitation or request, sir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm replying to the gentleman and giving him a proposal. Mr. Rajic could say, No, you must come to the meeting. And when Mr. Rajic learned that the joint statement was dated the 27th of March, then he also waited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't refuse anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Before I give Mr. Stojic the floor, who has a few things he would like to say, I will read out an oral decision on the Stojic and Petkovic requests and on the Prosecution request to have additional time for the cross-examination of Witness Pero Nikolic. The Witness Pero Nikolic, called by the Coric Defence, was initially to appear as a viva voce witness, whose examination-in-chief was to last for two hours. This witness will be now appearing pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules of the 25th of March, 2010. The Coric Defence has informed the Chamber and the parties of its intention to conduct an examination-in-chief for the duration of 30 minutes. In a motion filed on the 1st of February, 2010, the Prosecution requested two hours for the cross-examination of this witness. The Coric Defence, as well as the Praljak Defence, responded to this request, after which the Prosecution filed a response. In a motion dated the 3rd of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence asked for 20 minutes for the cross-examination of the witness. The Coric Defence responded to this request, and the Petkovic Defence then filed a response upon leave having been granted by the Chamber. In a motion dated the 5th of February, 2010, the Stojic Defence filed a request for 18 minutes for the cross-examination of the witness and asked that the additional time that might be allocated to it by the Chamber be deducted from the total amount of time it has been granted by the Chamber. The Coric Defence responded to the motion. Having examined the 65 ter summary and the 92 ter statement that concerns Pero Nikolic's testimony, as well as after having examined the parties' submissions, it is the Chamber's opinion that the Prosecution request is disproportionate, and believes that one hour should be sufficient for the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness in question. With regard to the requests for additional time filed by the Stojic and Petkovic Defence teams, the Chamber is of the opinion that 20 minutes for each Defence team should be sufficient for the cross-examination of the witness. The Chamber also takes note of the Stojic Defence request to have the additional time deducted from the total amount of time granted to it, and that will be six minutes. The Prlic Defence, Praljak Defence, and Pusic Defence have not filed any particular requests, and they will have 36 minutes that they should divide amongst themselves in order to conduct their cross-examination, if any. That is the oral decision concerning Witness Pero Nikolic. Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Very briefly, I would like to inform you of the fact that I've become a grandfather. I'm very happy today, and I wanted to share this good news with everyone in the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic, we've just found out about that, and we wish you all the best for the newborn child and for the child's family. We will now continue. Yes, Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving to Mostar around the 8th, 9th, and 10th of May, 1993, as I understand your testimony, sir, you've told this Chamber, under oath, that you were in Split the entire -- that entire period -- well, strike that. Not the entire period, but on the 8th and 9th, until later being called and coming to Mostar, that you were in Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Split, and I returned from Split. And then when we received information, Mr. Stojic and I returned from our trip to Tomislavgrad, we returned to Mostar. It was at 1.00 or 1.30. That's when I arrived in Mostar on that day, on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you go to Split, and when did you return -- well, I guess we now know, just to be clear. So you've just said you returned from Split to Mostar at approximately -- arriving at approximately 1.00 or 1.30. I'm not sure now, to be honest. In the morning or the afternoon of the 9th? You just said, sir, at least -- excuse me, excuse me, Mr. Petkovic, I apologise. Let me try to assist both of us. If the transcript is correct, it says that it was at 1.00 or 1.30 in the morning that you returned to Mostar, is that correct, or in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the afternoon, between 1.00 and 1.30. So it was in the afternoon on the 9th of May. That's when I arrived in Mostar. I arrived at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when had you gone to Split, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that between the time that you arrived in Split on the 7th and the time that you returned to Mostar on approximately -- at approximately 1.00 or 1.30 in the afternoon on the 9th, that you were not in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in Mostar. I arrived in Mostar for the first time between 1.00 and 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So eight hours after the beginning of the fighting, no, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you look, please, at P11179, which will be in the -- 11179. It will be binder number 2 of the second binder set, binder number 2. P11179. Sir, this is a BBC article that reports on a meeting by various members of the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities with a delegation from, at that time, European Community. P11 -- three 1s, P11179, of a meeting, sir. And if I can direct your attention to the first paragraph of the article, and the source of this, it's BBC, but it's reporting, if you look toward the bottom of the page, for those who might be interested, the actual source of the information is Croatian Radio Zagreb at 1500 Greenwich Mean Time on the 8th of May, 1993. According to this document, sir, this report, that the representatives of the HVO and the Herceg-Bosna that met with the European Community delegation included Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Petkovic, and an adviser to Mr. Boban, Pogarcic, on the 8th of May in Mostar. Sir, contrary to what you've told us so far under oath, you were in Mostar on the 8th of May, 1993, weren't you? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours, that's not correct. You've heard the testimony of Mr. Beese. I wasn't at a meeting in Mostar on the 8th of May, when there were three ambassadors present. I know about that. I heard about that later. This is a report from a journalist who wasn't familiar with the situation. Mr. Beese has testified here. He mentioned the people who attended the meeting. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to comment on this document and draw your attention to the fact that this BBC programme was broadcast on the 9th of May -- the 10th of May, 1993. That's what it says. It refers to sources of the 8th of May. I will correct line 5. It was broadcast on the 10th of May -- yes, it's been corrected. It refers to a source of the 8th of May. And then it's not clear, what the day refers to. "Today," this day, is it the day which it's broadcast or some other day? I think that this has to be clarified before we ask the witness where he was on that day. This isn't a matter of providing arguments. We're clarifying certain things. And, Mr. Scott, if you have two different dates, then we have to know what "today" means, which date is concerned. Did the BBC talk about what happened "today," on the 10th, or did they have the 8th of May in mind, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With great respect to my good friend Ms. Alaburic, the article is clear, and I said this a few moments ago, but I realise there's a lot going on in the courtroom. It is a BBC article dated the 10th. If you go to the bottom of the text, which frequently happens, one news service picks up a story from another news service source. Croatian Radio Zagreb, 1500 Greenwich Mean Time, 8th of May, 1993, and the Croatian Radio reporter says: "Slavko Ratko -- a report by Slavko Ratko from Herzegovina, president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, received in Mostar today ..." Now, Your Honours, I put it to you and I put it to the witness -- or I suggest to you and I put it to the witness that it's quite clear that the reference is to the 8th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were at that meeting, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Scott, I'll perhaps try and make a modest contribution. As far as I can remember, I believe that this was a protected witness, so I cannot mention the witness's name. But as far as I can remember, one of the three ambassadors referred to told us that he went to Mostar. It would be necessary to check the transcript, because he mentioned the day on which he arrived.
