I don't remember that he said that he arrived on the 8th of May, so we should check to see what the ambassadors say -- we should check to see what the ambassador said, because he participated in the meeting, attended the meeting, according to the BBC. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, I want to remind you that in this courtroom, under oath, Mr. Slobodan Bozic, the deputy minister of defence, Mr. Stojic's deputy, testified on the 3rd of February, 2009, transcript page 36267: "Q. Let's go back to the 8th of May, the preceding day of 1993. Do you recall where you were the day before the events of 9th of May? "A. Yes, I can remember that very well. In proofing for my testimony, I refreshed my memories. Of course, some dates needed no refreshing. On the day of the 8th of May, European Trojka diplomas, ambassadors of the presiding country of the EU, the previous holder of the Presidency and the next in line to take over the Presidency of the EU, came to Mostar, to Mr. Boban's office at the rector's office. Together with Mr. Boban, there was Mr. Prlic, Pogarcic, Mr. Stojic, General Petkovic, and myself. There was an afternoon meeting." Sir, a Defence witness in this case, who came into this courtroom and took an oath and told these Judges, said that you were at the meeting on the 8th of May, and you were, weren't you? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't at that meeting. You heard Mr. Beese's testimony here, and he mentioned the names of all those who attended the meeting. I didn't attend the meeting that was held on the 8th in Mostar. We can also check Mr. Beese's testimony. I think Mr. Beese testified here and mentioned the names of those who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that will be done, sir. You also then testified that you and Mr. Stojic were scheduled to meet with Mr. Siljeg on the 9th or 10th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Rama. Yes, it's the Tomislavgrad Military District. We were to go to Rama to see Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you did, in fact, go to -- not necessarily, perhaps not on the 9th, but around that time, that you did, in fact, go with Mr. Stojic to visit Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojic and I went to see Mr. Siljeg, and we then received information about 9.30 or 10.00 on Mr. Stojic's mobile phone according to which there was a conflict in Mostar. We then turned around, returned to Mostar, and arrived about 1.00 or 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you go to see Mr. Siljeg then sometime after that? Was the meeting essentially, if you will, rescheduled a day or two later?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember going to see Mr. Siljeg later because of the situation in Mostar. I went -- had negotiations with Halilovic and UNPROFOR. That went on for a few days, and as a result we didn't visit Mr. Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You see, sir, if you turn to -- if you'll now turn to Exhibit P02166, P02166, the first binder of this two-binder set, the last document in from the first binder, P02166. This is a diary of Mr. Siljeg, and if I can ask you to turn to the entries in his diary for the 8th and 9th of May, 1993. In the English version, it will be at page -- the 7th of May starts on the eighth -- excuse me, page 8. But you can find it by day, sir, in chronological order. If you turn to the 7th of May, 1993, and thereafter, I put it to you, sir, the Prosecution has reviewed these notes quite extensively, and I put to you that there is no record -- there is no indication in Mr. Siljeg's detailed notes of any planned meeting or actual meeting with you or Mr. Stojic on the 7th, 8th, or 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, because we didn't reach him. Ten kilometres before arriving, we returned, because we were provided with information according to which the situation had become difficult in Mostar, and we returned. So Siljeg can't say that we saw him. We didn't. We needed another 40 minutes -- we would have needed another 40 minutes to reach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see, and anyone in the courtroom can see by leafing through these various pages, Mr. Siljeg was a copious or detailed record-keeper, day by day. And I put it to you, sir, that if your minister of defence and your Chief of the Main Staff is coming to meet you, that's something that's quite noteworthy and would be in your agenda or your daily record. And there is nothing about any such meeting with you and Mr. Stojic around this time, scheduled or planned; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he wrote down. It's for him to decide, how to write his journal, what to put in his journal. I can't influence that. It's not an official document. He doesn't have a duty to make such entries. We went to see him, but we didn't reach him. The meeting with Siljeg didn't take place. I don't know how much time passed before someone met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was it -- was it part of the plan? Was there some sort of a discussion of some cover-up or plausible deniability, some might call it, that all the Herceg-Bosna and HVO authorities, the governmental authorities and the military authorities, you and Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic, and seemingly about everyone else, just either happened to be out of Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993, or at least claim to have been outside -- away from Mostar on the 9th of May? Is that something that there was discussion about beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a Sunday. On Sunday, in Mostar, there was no one, apart from those who were on duty, and Mr. Siljeg -- well, four or five days before, we'd worked in an area that bordered with his area, Konjic and Jablanica, and Mr. Siljeg asked us to visit him to see what we had been doing with Halilovic in the area of Konjic and Jablanica. Similarly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, sir, you've gone -- taken off and started talking on a completely irrelevant matter. I didn't ask you about any conversations you had with Mr. Siljeg four or five days before about that, in that respect. What I put to you, sir: Was there a discussion or are you telling this Chamber that it was just coincidence that on this extremely important day, the 9th of May, 1993, it appears that all the Herceg-Bosna HVO leadership claims -- either was or claimed to be out of Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on Friday evening, on Saturday and Sunday, no one stayed in Mostar, apart from those who were on duty. People would leave Mostar and go their various ways. The governmental officials would go home, and in the Main Staff you just had two or three people who remained. People just went home, and that was what happened after working hours. And every Saturday and Sunday, that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's stay on the topic of the 8th, 9th, 10th of May, 1993. There's been considerable testimony about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, having followed the questions -- or while following the questions and answers, I was going through Colonel Siljeg's notes. I had a look at the handwriting. Apparently, it's the same handwriting, so it should be him, it should be this person. I don't know how the Prosecution obtained this. Either it's from the archives or Colonel Siljeg was interviewed by the OTP and he, himself, provided these notes, but that's not my problem. I see that on the 6th of May, there was a meeting in Mostar. He wrote this down. The 6th of May, that's three days prior to the 9th of May. The 9th of May was a Sunday, the 8th of May a Saturday, the 7th of May a Friday, the 6th of May a Thursday; and, in fact, it does say "Thursday" here. So on this basis, I tell myself that if there's a plan, there has to be a trace of that plan. I can see two, four, six, eight items listed here, eight points. You can see A, B, C. If you want to have a look at the page, the page is 0402-1375, 0402-1419 in the English version. There's a request for two companies. There's the request for prisoners, communications, a tank. The military police has to obey orders. They have to establish the army in Jablanica. And then you have the Posusje Brigade. Well, when I see this, I can't see the traces of a plan. I can't see anything that refers to a plan of any kind. General Petkovic, have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, I haven't. This is Colonel Siljeg's notebook. On the 6th of May, he attended a meeting in Mostar. He mentioned certain problems, and we promised that we would go to Rama, where he was, and discuss each and every problem that he was facing. He made a list of his problems and of the subjects that we would have to discuss, and that was the purpose to go to see Colonel Siljeg on the 9th and to speak to him, and to try and solve his problems. But we didn't spend much time in Rama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, let's go to the heart of the matter. If the Prosecution allegation is correct that on the 9th of May the HVO attacked the ABiH, I would like to know whether, in military terms, on Thursday, when Siljeg was there, and he mentioned the meeting, would one have technically evoked the plan and the minutiae of the operations of the 9th of May? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no plan. Colonel Siljeg has just noted problems he is concerned with, things to do with the situation in his area. He's asking for 70 men, the Knez Domagoj Brigade to go to Klis. He wants the engineers to come to Prozor, and so on and so forth. These are things that he is requesting. He's requesting the Knez Domagoj Brigade that is to the south of Mostar, and if he is doing that, then there is no plans for Mostar or for anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting in Mostar, who attended the meeting, in your opinion, apart from Siljeg? Who could have attended it on the 6th of May? Because in the notebook it doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just myself. Colonel Siljeg came to have a meeting with me, and he mentioned his problems, because I hadn't seen Colonel Siljeg for a long time. I can't remember now, but perhaps we had no contact for 20 days. I was travelling through Central Bosnia with Halilovic and the international community representatives, and two days earlier we were perhaps 30 kilometres from Siljeg, when we were visiting the Konjic-Jablanica area. But we did not meet Colonel Siljeg. We didn't call him to the meeting that was attended by Halilovic and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have mentioned something that I was unaware of. You are saying that on -- you are saying that this meeting took place with you on the 6th of May, that the points mentioned were referred to -- were discussed at this meeting, but you didn't ask him for assistance for an operation on the 9th of May? Otherwise, there would be a written reference to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see that he is asking for some men from the Knez Domagoj Brigade. It's a unit that belongs to the Mostar Operative Zone. You can see that it says 70 men from Capljina, from the Knez Domagoj Brigade, to go to Klis. They are men going to Siljeg. They're not coming from Siljeg's area to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to add two questions on the 9th of May. The first is: I seem to have understood, but I would like you to clarify, that on the 6th of May, you made an appointment to visit Mr. Siljeg, and did you make an appointment to meet him on a certain day, which would be the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, on the 9th of May, because on the 10th of May, Halilovic and myself were to continue with our work in the Konjic-Jablanica area, and I think that it was on the 11th or 12th that we were supposed to promote a joint command in Mostar for this southern area. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, you were on your way to that meeting, and you decided otherwise. Did you inform Mr. Siljeg that you would not meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Siljeg was called from Mostar when we returned. We called him in the afternoon, said that we wouldn't be visiting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You say "we called him." I don't think that you were more than one person on the phone, or how do I have to understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "we," I'm thinking of the Main Staff. They sent Siljeg information stating that the general had returned, that he was in Mostar, and that he wouldn't be visiting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. So you had someone in your staff call him. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't really know, Judge Trechsel. The person who was manning the telephone was given the task of informing Siljeg that we had returned from our journey to Prozor and that we were in Mostar because of the situation that was taking place in the town of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all. I'm satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we were about to turn a few minutes ago to Exhibit P02019, P02019, which is in the first binder of the two-binder set that we've been working with today, the first binder. And while we're looking for that, sir, let me just set the scene, so to speak. There's been considerable evidence in the case about the whereabouts of Mr. Pasalic, the head of the ABiH 4th Corps, around the 7th, 8th, 9th of May, 1993. And I think you will recall that on that -- around that time, for a time he was isolated at a SpaBat base outside of -- some distance from Mostar. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't isolated at the time. Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Siber, as well as Mr. Filipovic, after Halilovic and I stayed in the Jablanica-Konjic area, Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Filipovic, on the 8th, in the afternoon, set out towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in the course of those events, he was subsequently isolated at a base, out of communication. HVO forces arrived and prevented Mr. Pasalic from leaving and, in fact, threatened to arrest him, except the Spanish Battalion commander would not allow that. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. I don't remember where they blocked him and when and how the HVO forces knew that Pasalic was in Dracevo. If they didn't know, you heard Filipovic say that they weren't able to leave and go out anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, sir, exactly. They were isolated. They were not able to communicate, they were not able to leave. And for the rest of it, we'll leave it for the Judges to recall and review the evidence, including the Spanish Battalion reports on these events. But if you look, sir, at P02019, isn't it the case, sir, that just a few days before this event happened, in fact, you had threatened to arrest Mr. Pasalic, and by doing so, to paralyse the 4th Corps of the ABiH by taking its commander out of pocket?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a meeting of the 21st of April in Vitez, and it has nothing to do with the 9th of May in Mostar, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, so you say, sir, so you say. But let's look at what you said, let's look at what you said. In the English version of the report -- this is a report from, excuse me, Mr. Blaskic to, among others, Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman to the chief of Military Intelligence, et cetera, dated the 21st of April, 1993. And there's a series of -- there's notes of the meeting. The first intervention -- the first comment is attributed to Mr. Thebault. Then there's Petkovic, then there's Blaskic, then there's Halilovic, and then there's Petkovic again. And it's the second Petkovic intervention that I want to focus on. At that time -- at that time, sir, you say: "I have no benefit from this piece of paper, the statement signed the previous evening." And I put it to you, sir, that takes us back to our topic earlier today about the often worthless value of so-called cease-fires: "I can see that this is a war, and, gentlemen, if you want a war, we will make sure that you get it. But you must realise that then there will be no Bosnian state and that you will not be able to cross the Kiseljak-Busovaca-Travnik road. "All we soldiers know, that troops do not move without orders from a commander ..." Et cetera. Skipping -- going over to the next page in the English version: "So I don't want to waste time with you, but remember that now I'm going to Mostar, and if you continue to attack the HVO, I will arrest Arif Pasalic and paralyse your 4th Corps, and you know I can easily do that." And, sir, that's exactly what you did two weeks later, isn't it, you and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not arrest Pasalic. Pasalic was taken by the Spanish Battalion of UNPROFOR and nobody could arrest him, so don't ascribe to us what the Spanish Battalion did quite improperly. And I'm saying this within the context of the arrest of Zivko Totic and my commander, Varisic [phoen], so two commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again you are taking us off subject, and you know it, because as soon as you want to go on something, you want to go on and talk about something else. I'm talking about Mr. Pasalic. And you know the evidence in this case, you were sitting in this courtroom, you've seen the Spanish Battalion reports, you've heard the evidence. Mr. Pasalic at the time was bottled up -- what some might say. He was bottled up in a Spanish Battalion camp, there were HV units outside that camp that would not allow him to leave. An HVO officer appeared at the Spanish Battalion camp, trying to arrest Mr. Pasalic, and the Spanish commander wouldn't do that. Now, he wasn't physically, at that point, put under arrest, but he was isolated, sir. He couldn't go anywhere. He was being held incommunicado, and you know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is they could leave him in Mostar, which they did not do, so let them answer why they did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking you the questions ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, it's not, sir. It doesn't matter what they could have done. It's what happened on the ground. And you know that he was at Dracevo, being bottled up by the HVO, and you know that. Don't tell me what somebody else could have done on another day, someplace else. He was sitting at the SpaBat base in Dracevo, bottled up by HVO forces that wouldn't allow him to leave and, in fact, tried to arrest him. And that's the simple truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The HVO, also around this time-period, arrested Mr. Pasalic's wife; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- tried to provide a response when the Prosecution is putting something to the witness. If you check the transcript, my dear colleague first put one fact in front of the witness, then another fact, and now he's going on a third fact, and the witness still didn't -- still didn't got the opportunity to say at least, No. Nothing was allowed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacic. Did you look at page 61, lines 13, 15? I'm not going to cross-examine you, but what I read there is, "No," and then again, "No, it's not true." So I find it difficult to understand why you say that he did not even have the chance to say, No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The witness started with: "No, and ..." He wanted to add, I don't know, maybe two words, maybe five words, maybe two sentences. But the Prosecutor didn't give him the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you told us that the witness did not even have the chance to say, No. Well, that was not correct, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, this, No, was not ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's go on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: ... if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By this time, or at least by the time we get to December of 1993, the HVO was holding Mr. Pasalic's wife also, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Pasalic's wife lived in a flat on the west bank, and from the 30th of June, Mr. Pasalic lived on the east bank, and that's the whole truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit P07028. It's in the second binder of the two-binder set, P07028. This is a document from Rasim Delic on the 4th of December, 1993: Attention, 4th Corps Command: "Major General Milivoj Petkovic, deputy commander of the HVO, gave guarantees that he will release Arif Pasalic's wife and hand her over to UNPROFOR Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje, which is supposed to transport her to Jablanica. "This assignment should be carried out in the next two or three days ..." And directing your attention to the end of that paragraph: "For the purpose of carrying out this assignment, commission representatives shall make contact with Mr. Berko Pusic and monitor the completion of the assignment." You gave a guarantee to Mr. Delic or his representative, at some point in late November or early December of 1993, that you would release Mr. Pasalic's wife, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Delic talked to me about the problem of Mr. Pasalic's wife, who was living on the right bank, and I said I would do anything in my power for Mrs. Pasalic, if she so desires, could meet with Pasalic, her husband, wherever she wants. And Delic said that the best thing would be for the Spanish Battalion to be involved, and he was involved, and to inform the MUP where the lady was, in what flat. And with the help of the Spanish Battalion, as Delic asked, she was transferred to Jablanica, and that's the truth of the whole situation about Mrs. Pasalic. She wasn't imprisoned. She was living in a flat in West Mostar, and she was found two or three hours later -- they reached her two or three hours later, and she accepted the offices of the Spanish Battalion and left for Jablanica, because that's what Mr. Delic had requested. Nothing more than that, that's all. So those were my services.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on to the subject of the camps briefly. Just a couple of questions there. Sir, you testified at transcript page 49578. You were making reference to a conversation allegedly with Mr. Boban, and you gave this testimony: "He --" And I put it to you, sir, the record will clearly reflect it was

utterances.speaker: MR. BOBAN
utterances.text: "He said that the HVO had facilities that can put up this number of men, and that it was up to the army to disarm these men in the safest manner, and everybody else was somebody -- oh, sorry. Everything else was for somebody else to take care of." And this was all in reference to the arrest of the Muslim men, starting in early July 1993. You said: "Everything else -- after disarming them, everything else was for somebody else to take care of." I'd like you to tell the Judges, who was the "somebody else," because someone has to take responsibility for the detaining and detention and holding of these thousands of Muslim men, so who was it, if it's not you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't me, and the Main Staff had nothing to do with that. The Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was? My question is very clear: Who was?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decree provided for the fact that the Defence Centre should -- Defence Department should deal with centres of that kind. And you saw that we had detainees and that they were held in military investigative prisons, and they were places where both prisoners were held and detainees and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're saying, sir, that the responsibility for these detained and imprisoned Muslim men was with Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that it was the Defence Department. Now, who Mr. Stojic was dealing with, that's -- that was up to him. The HVO had military investigative centres and a central prison and others which, in 1992, prisoners and detainees -- prisoners of the Serb army and detainees and members of the HVO were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's quite correct, sir, and I think it's worthwhile for the courtroom to remember that. Holding the Muslims in 1993 was not the first time that the HVO had held prisoners, because you were holding Serbs in 1992 at many of these same camps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were at war with the Serbs, and there were prisoners of war, and they kept in military investigative prisons, not camps of any kind. They were military investigative prisons that existed in the Mostar-Capljina-Ljubuski area, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that even in 1992, various international agencies and reporters, including Mr. Mazowiecki, reported abuses and mistreatment in connection with the HVO's holding of the Serbs in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my information goes, and as far as I was able to learn, I don't think there was any abuse or mistreatment of those prisoners, whether they be Serbs or anybody else; and that they were regularly exchanged on the basis of negotiations and talks, and that the exchanges took place, I think it was, in October of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back to July of 1993. So you've told us that it was Mr. Stojic's Defence Department that was responsible. What steps did you take -- as the head of the HVO and, in fact, the head of the military detaining authorities, what steps did you take to assure yourself that these men, arrested under your authority, were being properly treated, properly housed in proper conditions, properly classified, as required by the Geneva Conventions, and properly treated? What steps did you take to ensure yourself that that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, steps like that were not prescribed under the responsibility of the Croatian Defence Council. The HVO would hand over soldiers taken prisoner at places prescribed and where they should be handed over, and further proceedings did not come under the HVO's responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your answer is, sir, that to your knowledge, that wasn't done? Certainly, you didn't do it, and, to your knowledge, nobody did it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that they didn't do that. You can follow the situation from October. The areas were toured and visited, and solutions were looked into --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir. No, sir. I'm talking about July 1993, sir. And you were the head -- you were still at that moment the head of the HVO. You had responsibility, under International Law to take steps to ensure that these men, arrested under your authority, were then housed and treated properly. And I want you to tell these Judges, under oath, what due diligence you exercised to make sure that that was the case in July 1993. I'm not talking about October. I want you to talk to these Judges about July 1993 and what specific steps you took.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking quite specifically. My remit and authority was only to hand over the detainees and isolated to the centres. I had no authority under any provisions to do anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I take it your answer to my question is: You didn't do anything, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't come under my responsibility, and I didn't interfere in the affairs of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to the topic of forced labour of many of these men after they were being held. You were on notice throughout this period that people being held by the HVO were being used for forced labour and were being injured and sometimes even killed in the course of forced labour? You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the labour, but I had no information telling me that somebody had been killed. No information like that reached the Main Staff of the HVO from those who were in charge of the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I inform Mr. Petkovic and the Chamber and all those in the courtroom that we're now going to be working out of a binder that is titled "Tables - Forced Labour and Military Discipline and Justice."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can start, please, as everyone is orienting themselves to that binder. If we can start, please, by looking at 1D02447. It will probably be the last part of that first divider. There's some green dividers in the binder as well, but this should be the last document prior to one of the green dividers. Sir, this document is -- represents or memorialises the agreements of various of the parties to the recognition and application of the Geneva Conventions. And if I can just turn your attention to the signature page, you will see that that is signed -- apologies. Let me back up to the first page first. On the first page, there is a list of names, and it says that for the president of the Croatian Democratic Community, it says: "Representative, Mr. Miljenko Brkic, president," and his representative being Mr. Sito Coric. And is it correct that that's the brother of the Mr. Coric that is one of the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document. Otherwise, I didn't know about the meeting. Well, I don't see when it was held, I don't see a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at the last page, on the signature page, I believe that you'll see it was held and signed on the 22nd of May, 1992. But, sir, you were aware then -- you said you didn't know that the prisoners were being killed, but you -- that prisoners had been killed, excuse me, but that forced labour was going on, and at least some had been injured, to your knowledge, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a single report. I'm not saying that there weren't people who had been wounded, but I don't remember any report addressed to me saying that something like that had happened from the detention centres. I said I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P02950 in that same binder, the one we're now working in, P02950. This is a report from the ICRC, dated the 25th of June, 1993, addressed to Mr. Blaskic, but also copied to you, sir. We see in the c.c.'s Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Petkovic and others. And it's reported to you, sir, and the others copied: "The ICRC is preoccupied by the ongoing practice of detaining authorities according to which prisoners are regularly being sent for work to areas exposed to the danger of fightings. This has again led to the wounding and death of prisoners held in detention places under HVO authority." Skipping a paragraph: "Such a practice is a serious break --" perhaps "breach of the Geneva Conventions. It is unacceptable and has to be stopped at once." You received that report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this, and this is a report for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't care where it's for. You --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I look at the whole document so that I could look it up in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask for the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but while we're looking for the document, I wanted to deal with this during the break with Mr. Scott, because there's obviously a mistake. I don't know whether there was a mistake in the translation, too. But, anyway, in the previous document, 1D02447, mention is made of somebody called Sito Coric, and it's obviously not Mr. Valentin Coric. And on page 68 of the transcript, in lines 10, 11, it says -- the question was: "Is that Mr. Coric who is one of the accused in this case?" Obviously, it's somebody different, so maybe Mr. Scott made a mistake, and we could correct the transcript to avoid any misunderstanding later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I misspoke, I apologise, but perhaps, with apologies, it was just not heard correctly. I believe I said, Do I understand correctly that that's the brother of Mr. Valentin Coric. I think that's what was proper, and if it wasn't on the record, that's certainly what I thought I said and intended to say, but not Mr. Valentin Coric. I never -- I had no intention to indicate that it was Mr. -- this Mr. Coric, but his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've had a chance to look at P02950. I would like you now to go to P07 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to get this clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is of no relevance for us at all, whether it's a brother, a cousin, or someone completely unrelated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only a point of curiosity, perhaps, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at P07660, a report to you, sir, dated the 24th of January, 1994, you and Mr. Jukic and Mr. Pogarcic and Mr. Prlic, in which it is indicated, again: "Sir, it is with great concern that the ICRC has learned that prisoners are again being used for work on the front-line." Now, do you remember that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The 24th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm seeing the translation as being the 11th or November. Well, I can assume that this was sent to these addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will go, please, sir, to -- well, before we get to that, as I understand your testimony, sir, you don't deny that with your knowledge, forced labour of Muslim -- detained and held Muslims was taking place, that the HVO was using detained Muslims, whether they be prisoners, detainees, people that were not at liberty, were using those -- the HVO was using those people for forced labour. I understand that you are not denying that; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, detainees were taken out for labour. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to be clear, because I maybe wasn't clear what you were saying a few days ago. Were you saying that it was only detained Muslim members of the HVO who were being sent for forced labour at the front-line or that any and all detained or imprisoned or held Muslims of any sort, so to speak, were being also sent to perform forced labour at and around the front-line?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I have reviewed, and seen the documents here, the word used is "detainees," and these are soldiers of the HVO. That is what is stated on the documents allowing those people to be used for labour. We've looked at I don't know how many documents, and everywhere, as far as I can remember, it says "detainees."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look, for example, at Exhibit P04020. There is a -- I should have said, Your Honours, and because we're trying to move -- at least I'm trying to move quickly, there is also a table attached to or that accompanies this set of documents which is a -- has 20 -- excuse me, has 32 items entitled "Forced Labour," and obviously, it goes without saying, we don't have time to go through each one of them. I've just referred you to P04020, which is in the table, just by way of reference, at table line 9. Sir, this was an order of yours on the 8th of August, 1993, in which you specifically authorised the use -- and I'm looking at item number 1: "Fortify the achieved lines immediately. Prisoners and detained Muslims may be used for fortifying lines." Now, sir, that seems to suggest to me that Muslims of any sort, essentially, prisoners or detained Muslims, were being used and sent to the front-lines to engage in forced labour, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what was done in the detention centre, which category the people belonged to. What is important is what was done in the detention centres and which were the people who were separated for work, for labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what steps did you take to ensure that the proper procedures were followed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When checking these things, we can see that these were people who were detained. And, secondly, these people were 15 or 20 kilometres away from the closest line of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask the same question, sir: What steps did you take to ensure yourself that these prisoners were being treated properly and that any particular group of prisoners were going or not going? Because here you were very clear. You talked about two different groups, prisoners and detained Muslims. As far as you were concerned, they could both go and fortify -- fortify the achieved lines, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the detention centre the people would be selected, and when I looked at the list, these were all people who enjoyed the status of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to put it to you -- to remind you of your testimony in the Kordic case. If we could have slide 30, please. At page -- transcript page 26774-75, the same document was put to you: "A. Your Honours, yes, I signed the order. This was in response to the work of Croats in Neretva River Valley and in Mostar who were digging fortifications on front-lines as prisoners ... this was my response to what was happening on the other side." So you were saying, sir, that, well, because the other -- at least according to you or according to this statement, because the other side was doing it, you were going to do it too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such instances, and unfortunately such things happened too. When one side saw the other side doing something, then they also would do the same. And I stand by what I said about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you know full well, sir, and you knew then because of your JNA training, and you certainly know after sitting in this courtroom for almost four years, tu quoque is not a defence by any means. Now, whether I agree -- whether we agree for the moment whether the Muslims were doing it or not, taking it for the moment that they were arguendo, that provided you no legal justification or justification at all for engaging in that practice, did it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It need not be, nor must they do what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, sir, that detained ABiH members, people -- ABiH -- Muslim ABiH members who had been held -- were being held by the HVO were being sent to engage in forced labour at the front-lines, and not just detained Muslim members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that there weren't any such instances, but the absolute majority of those people were members of that brigade or the adjoining brigade, people who used to be in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you might not recall the specifics, sir, and that would be understandable, but I would indicate to you and to the courtroom that in Exhibit P10206 and P09200, which are under seal, and I'm not going to refer to any of the specific information, but the statements of ABiH members, admitted in this case, who were sent to perform forced labour on the front-lines, you wouldn't disagree with that, would you, that that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that there may have occasionally been such instances, and I don't know how they stated that they were members of the ABiH, because many who were in the HVO made statements saying that they were members of the ABiH; whereas, in fact, their real status was that they were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The real problem -- or part of the real problem here, sir, is that, contrary to the requirements of International Law, the HVO had not classified the various held persons properly, whether they were civilian detainees, prisoners of war, held HVO members. That just simply hadn't taken place. And, in fact, you're in no position, are you, sir, to give this Chamber any assurances which of the Muslims being held were sent for forced labour because they had never been classified, and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The classification had started, but every member of the HVO stated, himself, that he was a member, so it was possible to establish with precision that he was a member of the HVO, because, after all, it was in most cases former members of the HVO that were being looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Being looked for." What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that people who were looked for to work were, in the vast majority of cases, members of the HVO. I'm not denying that there may have been some others, but I will not confirm it either. In any way, it was the people who had been in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. You've told us several times now in the last hour, under oath -- my apologies, Judge Prandler. Sorry. Sir, you've told us several times in the last hour, under oath, that once these men were arrested and disarmed, you turned them over and washed your hands of them and had nothing to do with it; rightly or wrongly, you had nothing more to do with them. So how can you turn around and tell this Chamber and assure this Chamber of which prisoners actually went out and whether they were properly classified or not? You were either involved in it, sir, or you weren't. And you either took responsibility and did what's required under International Law or you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved. But according to all the documents we've reviewed, one can see that they were exclusively detained members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're saying the documents you've reviewed in preparing to testify; that's what you're telling us? Is that what we're to understand? It's not what you knew at the time, but it's the defence that you've prepared now?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a part of the facts from the people who were looking for their soldiers. The people I had contact with, they were all looking for their soldiers, and everything else I saw from the documentation. They were those who had the status of detained soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After your 14th of October, 1993 order, which we've seen in the courtroom, in which you prohibited -- asserted to prohibit the continued use of forced labour except with your approval, the reality is, sir -- the plain reality is that practice continued in a widespread and systematic manner, and you knew about it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it. I sent an order, and every person in charge of detention should have observed it. And we saw that in the testimony of one of them, he violated my order and he gave soldiers to the 3rd Brigade. According to him, this was within the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look very quickly, please, in the table at what -- at lines 20, 21, 22, and 23, which, for the record, are respectively P07878, P05882, P08043, and P05895. All documents after your 14th October order, all plainly indicating the continued use of Muslims in forced labour; correct? Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these data show that there were such instances, and we also saw the documents for each specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, I note two statements of yours on pages 74 and 75. And as they give the impression of a contradiction which you had perhaps not intended to make, I would like to give you the opportunity to set this right. On page 74, lines 19 and following, especially 19 to 22, you said: "Many who were in the HVO made statements saying that they were members of the ABiH." And on the following page, 75, line 7 and following, I read: "Every member of the HVO stated, himself, that he was a member, so it was possible to establish with precision that he was a member of the HVO." Now, it seems to me that that's not the same, because first you said that many members of the HVO said that they weren't members and wrongly stated that they were members of the ABiH; whereas in the second statement you seem to say that if someone said he was a member of the HVO, he could be trusted, that would be true. Can you clarify us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there must have been an error. I said that members of the HVO said that they were members of the HVO. They never said that they were members of the army. So who was in the HVO, in his statement there he claimed to have been a member of the HVO, and he said which brigade he had been a member of. Maybe there's a misinterpretation. So not a single member of the HVO did not say that he was a member of the army, but, rather, he said he was a member of the HVO, even indicating the brigade he belonged to. I don't know what the other point was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, first you had said that there -- occasionally they stated that they were members of the ABiH, because many who were in the HVO made statements saying that they were members of the ABiH. And that, of course, is not the same. But you would then withdraw this first statement, or -- if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not members of the -- sorry, of the army. They stressed that they were members of the HVO, and they indicated which brigade they belonged to and when they joined the HVO. So these people, themselves, said that they were members of the HVO, which brigade they belonged to, and when they had joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as always, of course, I'm in the Chamber's hands, but I'm about to start the last topic and it might be just as well to take -- if it's acceptable, to take the break now and then come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But just a question before we have the break. I was looking at all the documents regarding labour that are in the Prosecutor's binder, and one document -- and I'll give you the reference, P042, P042 [as interpreted]. Please look at this document for a particular reason. It's an order, and it's addressed to the operational zone. But what drew my attention to it was that you say it is necessary to fortify the lines and that prisoners and Muslim detainees should be used for the fortification of the lines. So we understand what you're saying, but you add -- and this is rather important because it may be a point of dispute with Mr. Coric, you add the following, and I read: "Ask permission from the military police (who are in charge of the use of prisoners)." When I saw this phrase, I asked myself, What does this mean? Did you have the legal capacity to say that such and such prisoners would go to such and such place for labour, or you did not have such competence, and who did have that capacity was only the military police? What text are you relying on when you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was drafted by Mr. Zarko Tole. I signed it. And he felt that these centres, especially Heliodrom, are within the competence of the military police, and that is what he said, that the military police should be addressed. And I signed such a document without, to be quite frank, looking closely at what it said in the first item. But a request may be made by anyone, but the warden of the detention centre is the one who may say, You do not have the right to do this, and that's the end of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now the responsibility is being sent to the director of the prison, or the warden. Let me take a case, a particular case. You need three soldiers, prisoners, for cleaning the road. Do you have the ability to take them from the Heliodrom to have them clean the road or do you have to have permission from the military police and permission from the director of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Requests were mainly addressed to the prison warden. In this specific case, I don't know what the procedure was, but all requests were addressed directly to the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question: If here the warden had said, No, could you have over-stepped his decision or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If he refuses to give the prisoners, then you couldn't take them. Whoever was refused, he came back without the requested number of soldiers. And there were such cases when the warden, especially respecting my order, for a few days after my order he would refuse all such requests as a matter of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you have said is in the transcript. Yes, Mr. Scott, you wish to make a follow-up question or shall we have the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can have the break, Your Honour. But just before the break, I just want to do correct -- make a transcript correction. The document that Your Honour has been referring to for the past few minutes was recorded on page 79, line 1, as "P042." It should obviously be P04020. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right. Let's have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, before we go forward, I did come back and see a couple of things that I wanted to touch on, on forced labour, before we go forward. Could I ask you, please, to look at P05308, which again will be in the same binder that we've been working in this morning or most recently, P05308, about halfway through that first section before the first green -- before the first green divider. While you're doing that, sir: This is a report from the ICRC, dated the 23rd of September, 1993, and it appears to be, sir, directly addressed to you about forced labour. You recall receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll up a bit, please? No, could I see the other page to see to whom it was addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the English version, for these purposes, I think you'll see your name at the bottom left-hand side of the document. Sir, I'd like to save some time. My question to you is just simply: Do you recall receiving that report, dated the 23rd of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say whether I received it or not, but here it says that it was addressed to me. But I can't say whether I received it or not, but as far as I can see it is addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And similarly, sir, if we could turn to P05967, it should be fairly close by, P05967, this is a further report dated the 20th of October, 1993, and I again put it to you, sir, that under the signature -- information, it is again addressed to you, isn't it? It's addressed to you, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you recall receiving this document --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that it's addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall receiving this report, dated the 20th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember whether I received the document or not because you don't have a stamp on the document that shows that it was received in the Main Staff. The reports sent by international representatives were quite numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you agree with me, sir, that while you may not specifically recall receiving these particular documents, it's likely, in the normal course of business, letters coming to you -- coming in from international organisations, addressed to you, that in the normal course of business you would and did receive them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If it was addressed to me, I would receive the report, and if it arrived in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last question, I believe, about camps and forced labour, but more specifically camps: Mr. Praljak testified during his examination that at the time of the hand-over, if you will, around the 24th of July, 1993, that he had no briefing from you, no conversations with you, about the camps, either Heliodrom, Ljubuski, Dretelj, Gabela, do you agree with Mr. Praljak or do you confirm that at the time of the turn-over, you gave him no briefing on the camps, or is Mr. Praljak wrong? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss this subject, because four hours after the hand-over of power, we interrupted the briefing, Praljak then went to Prozor because of the situation with Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, turning to the area of crimes and responsibility, I want to put to you, as a starting point on this, and I'll tell you and tell the courtroom I believe this will be our last topic. My review of the documents and your prior testimony in Kordic and Blaskic indicates, if I understand correctly, sir, your basic position or your starting point as to command and military discipline is that you, as a commander, had authority over those in your command, and as part of that authority, either explicitly or implicitly, you had the authority to take measures to exercise that command, in other words, to make it real, didn't you, or is that your starting point?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had authority over my commanders. But as for legal authority, no, I didn't have the legal authority to punish such a commander, to strip him of his rank, to place him in detention, and to take other similar measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's quickly look at two of your statements in the Blaskic case. If we can put Sanction slide 14, please. First from Blaskic transcript 24145: "... as commander, I proceed from the fact that all units within my territory are under my command and that I have certain authority over them." And at the Blaskic transcript 24023: "So anybody making problems should be arrested and prosecuted." Do you stand by both of those statements and make those statements the same today as your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it should have been, that one had to know who had the authority to arrest and to detain someone. That's why certain laws and regulations were drafted, and it is explicitly stated what the responsibility of each individual is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to spend a few minutes, what we have left remaining, looking at another table which is titled "Military Discipline and Justice." It's in the same binder that we've been working in. It will be behind the first -- the green divider, so to speak, behind the green divider, table, "Military Discipline and Justice." Sir, I'd just like to at least like to cover the heading just to confirm -- I'm hoping that perhaps these won't be matters of particular dispute, at least in general, but nonetheless, under each of the headings we've tried to present a number of documents that we submit support that particular section, if you will. Do I understand correctly that an HVO commander had the authority and the ability to issue orders arresting, suspending, and holding an HVO officer or soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detaining soldiers, well, the Chief of the Main Staff didn't have such authority to detain soldiers, but he could issue an order according to which a certain commander should be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for example, line 1, and we actually saw this earlier in different context, P01344, you had issued an order to Siljeg: "1. Arrest and imprison all our extremists." So I take it, sir, when you issued that order, you thought you had authority to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did that. At least that's what it says in the report that was submitted in the following few days. It said that the order had been carried out and that certain men had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as another example, line 4 of the table, P10308, order from Petkovic dated the 15th of May, 1993: "I hereby order suspension from duty for the following persons:" And, in fact, you suspended, I believe, 12 HVO members on your order, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see where that is. Which document did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P10308 in that same section of the binder behind the table, before the end. It's almost next to last, sir. You order suspension from duty of a number of HVO soldiers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I had to withdraw that order two or three days later because here it concerns Bujo [as interpreted] Bosnjak and others. Bujo [as interpreted] Bosnjak was a SIS member, and I had to withdraw this order because I didn't have the authority to suspend him. Two or three days later, I believe that I cancelled this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look at line 7, please, P01598, an order from you dated the 3rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. As we are meticulous, I think it's our task, you are recorded as saying that you had to withdraw the order regarding Bujo Bosnjak, but there is no Bujo Bosnjak on this list. There is only Zeljko Bosnjak. Was that -- did you misspeak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says "Zeljko Bosnjak - Lujo," and I used this abbreviated name. It says, as you can see, "Zeljko Bosnjak - Lujo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right, I see that. And then it was understood as being "Bujo," so one can see how linguistic problems can -- thank you for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I may interrupt, there is an error in transcript, page 85, 23, the response of General Petkovic until the second line of the next page. He said clearly, on our language, that Mr. Bosnjak was an officer of SIS. This is what I understood, and I think it was also in English I heard it, but it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go to line 7, P01598, this is an order from you, sir, dated the 3rd of March, 1993, providing that: "Due to reasonable suspicion that he abused his official position as an HVO," I believe that's a typo, "HVO GS officer, abused the official stamp, and tried forcibly to take someone's apartment, I hereby order: Arrest the officer Ante Ivankovic and investigate the above-mentioned circumstances." You confirm having issued that order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go forward, you mentioned the other day that there had been no disciplinary -- no courts had been established, no military disciplinary courts, and I want to make sure that we haven't misunderstood that. As I understand it, sir, and I'm asking -- you can correct me if I'm wrong, when you're talking about military disciplinary courts, these were military panels to formally -- if requested, to formally hand out military discipline, but this is something distinct and separate from the district military courts, the actual judicial courts, and those did exist, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those were misdemeanor courts -- these were penal courts, and the other was disciplinary, and it was never established in the HVO. That's the difference between the two courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in reality, sir, the non-existence of these disciplinary courts, as opposed to what I'm going to call the military district courts -- excuse me, Counsel. If I can just finish my question, possibly. If it's a correction in the transcript, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that it could lead to further misunderstandings. This is line 16. The transcript said "those were misdemeanor courts and those were penal courts." Those which is translated as misdemeanor, as it was earlier translated, those were disciplinary courts, and this is the distinguish [sic] we usually have. Now, we introduce misdemeanor courts, which is essentially very similar, but it may -- it may create confusion. So better to stick to classification which we already had. Criminal penal courts, on one side, and disciplinary courts, on the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would be the division. There would be the disciplinary courts and there would be the penal or criminal courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, again, just so the courtroom is not misled, the criminal courts, those did exist and were operating, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such military courts did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the non-existence of these military disciplinary bodies really had no practical effect, did they, because essentially a commander at the various levels could establish or implement or carry out the same forms of discipline with or without those disciplinary panels, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really say, sir. There's a difference between disciplinary procedure and disciplinary violations. For example, in the Republic of Croatia, there were military disciplinary courts that dealt with the majority of cases, but in the HVO there was no disciplinary military court, and that was a significant obstacle for commanders at all levels when it came to -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- correcting certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hear you. But as we look at this table, until we get down to the actual referral to a criminal prosecutor and the military disciplinary courts, the non-existence of these disciplinary bodies did not prevent you or any other HVO commander from carrying out the various forms of discipline that we see here; suspending officers and soldiers from duty, we've already talked about that. Number 2 -- heading number 2: "Orders detaining an HVO soldier -- officer or soldier for up to 15 days. "Orders imposing detention/imprisonment of more than 15 days. "Orders imposing some form of physical punishment." And we can see examples, in fact, as extreme as to be executed by shooting, according to Mr. Praljak on the 28th of July, 1993, at line 10. Number 5: "Orders imposing any sort of financial penalty or fines, such as withholding pay." We have an example of that: "Ordering relieving and removing officer or commander on duty." We have examples of that: "Orders disbanding a unit." And we have an example and others, actually, that we don't have time to get to that are in the table of that. But all those things could be done, and, in fact, as indicated by the documents, were done; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases, yes, discipline of that kind was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally we have: "Orders and referrals for investigation and prosecution," heading, if you will, number 8. And those, we can agree, when there would be something going to the military prosecutor and the military court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along with a criminal report, it goes to the military prosecutor or, rather, the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to Exhibit 4D01078, binder 3. Sorry -- I'm sorry for the logistics, but it's the third binder, labelled "Binder 3," in fact. We might have to go back and forth between those two a bit. If you look at 4D01078, sir, and if we can put Sanction slide 40 up as well, please. This is a report that you made to Mr. Boban on the 23rd of April, 1993, a fairly important period in our case; and in that report, sir, to Mr. Boban, among other things -- and I'm going to work from the Sanction slide, according to my notes. In that document you report to Mr. Boban, among other things: " ... some parts of HVO, private and village groups, incited by extremists, committed terror acts against civilians and destroyed great numbers of housing facilities. Actually, some settlements were completely burned down." You also report that: "... there are occurrences of massacring of civilians." You also report that: "From Kiseljak to Kobiljaca, towards Sarajevo, more than 60 Muslim houses were burned down, men captured, and women and children left in those burned areas. You also report that: "Three days ago, 250 Muslims have been expelled from Vitez and Busovaca. Car bomb in Vitez was sent from 'our side' into Muslim part. So far there are information on 10 casualties, number of wounded persons and number of devastated houses." You reported that: " ... the fact is that these events will cause great damage to us." You reported that: "The Muslim people, both military and civilian structures, perceive HVO as enemy army." You report to Mr. Boban: " ... Muslim villages are taken over and each village would then be burned down, and killings were committed uncontrollably." Sir, you knew, when you reported -- made this report to Mr. Boban toward the end of April, 1993, that the HVO was having -- had a major problem with crimes being committed against Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't check everything, but I accepted the information as I received it, and I informed Mr. Boban about everything that I saw when I was in Central Bosnia or my observations, and also in Northern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, based on your knowledge of these matters, not in this particular report but more generally, these HVO crimes could not be blamed simply on the random acts of individuals, that some of these crimes -- some of these practices were being carried out on a widespread and systematic basis, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't agree with you there, because all the information that I received from these people, regardless of the fact that they weren't checked out, indicated that they were groups that were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, that's always the -- that's always the excuse, though, isn't it? That's the story. I mean, if it's your side -- if there's misconduct on your side, it's out-of-control groups, but in the case of -- in your case, for instance, if it was the Muslims and Serbs, if there's misconduct on their side, it's all highly co-ordinated, top-down, policy-driven; that's always the way it is, isn't it? And if we were in a courtroom with Serb perpetrators, they'd say the same thing, that, All Serb crimes were individual bad actors, but, You know, those Croats, it was top-down, highly co-ordinated. I mean, that's the way it's played out, isn't it, sir? Every side says, Our crimes were uncontrolled elements, your crimes were intentional top-down policy-driven; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is information which I took on board, and people said there was uncontrolled behaviour, and that Blaskic, faced with a situation like that, couldn't put a stop to individuals acting that way. And then I said to Blaskic that, Such individuals must be stopped, even if you have to use weapons to stop them. And I presented all this to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some testimony and some of your -- another prior statement of yours on Sanction slide 43, please. Your testimony in the Kordic case, at transcript page 26746, and we may have touched on this earlier, but we come back to it: "Your Honours, yes. Every unit had to be under somebody's control; it could not exist on its own and act on its own." And then in an interview you gave in May 1993, which is marked as P00999, you said: "A unit, even the smallest one, is under the control of either one or the other side, so that their units, everything they do, cannot be justified as being out of control." That's what you said. You made both of those statements, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about units. When I say "units," they have their organisational establishment, and that's the units I mean. So companies, squads, whatever, they have their organisational establishment. Ones that do not are the ones that I considered to be outside that structure. So every organisational unit, from squads, companies, and so forth, platoons, must be organised and have supervision. Those who are not within that scope are out of control, and there are no two ways about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, when this Chamber is reviewing the evidence in this case, and there is an act of expulsion, or an act of killing, or an act of destruction, or an act of assault or mistreatment being carried out by an HVO units, those were not units out of control, they were units for which you were responsible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the units who, in organisational establishment terms, belonged to someone, they were under control. When I mentioned these others, I mean units outside any control. They do not belong to the HVO, in establishment terms, and are not in the establishment of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I'm putting to you now, sir -- putting aside whether I agree with you or not, at least as to the HVO units, the way you've defined them, you agree, don't you, and I believe you've just told us so, that as to the HVO units, they had to be considered and were considered under control and for which the HVO command would be and was responsible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who were under control and were in the establishment, the command is in control of them, or should be, from top to bottom and bottom to top, so they are units which must have somebody responsible. Each such unit must have somebody in command of it, responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that responsibility then goes up the HVO chain of command, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, wasn't it often the case, sir, talking about these alleged uncontrolled units, that that was often a convenient excuse or even a manipulation of events to blame things or just tell the internationals, Well, you know, that was only an uncontrolled unit or uncontrolled individuals? Was that often carried out as kind of a ploy?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We knew that the units that were under command were stated that they were under command and control. Nobody lied about Ahmici and said that there were some units outside that brought in or that the bomb -- truck bomb was not placed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The truck bomb in Stari Vitez, that's what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it says that it was one of our units -- one of our units was there, and everything else that was out of control were not those that belonged to us. So what the HVO was registered and recorded, and it was presented to the internationals, and ultimately they toured all the area with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. If you can look, please, at Sanction slide 44, which comes from Exhibit P04792. This is an order issued by Zarko Tole, one of the -- perhaps one might consider him number 3 in the HVO after you and

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Tomorrow, 5 September 1993, stop all movement of UN, UNHCR, and UNPROFOR at the military police check-points in your area of responsibility ... prevent all movements towards Jablanica and the South-East Operative Zone. These activities are to continue up until 1500 hours. Number 2: "This is to be carried out as to look as if it was the result of the arbitrary behaviour of the check-point policemen, while we should appear as doing everything to let them get through." And you know, sir, that sort of ploy wasn't uncommon at all, was it? It's all too convenient to just say, Well, you know, those guys are just out of control, but that's not really what we wanted them to do, but, in fact, Mr. Tole told them exactly what to do, Stop all movement of UN, UNHCR, et cetera, vehicles, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on what occasion Mr. Tole wrote that. I haven't found the document to read it from start to finish, to see under what circumstances he made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P04792, it's in the same section of the binder that we've been looking at -- it's in the binder 3. The document, frankly, is not much longer than the parts that are on the screen. It's a very short document. You can't find it. I think you have it now.
