In fact, sir, do you recall that this was around the time that Mr. Praljak was engaged in an HVO offensive around Gornji Vakuf on the 4th, 5th, 6th, around that time, of 1993, and it was Mr. Praljak that didn't want the internationals moving around and checking on things while the HVO was conducting this offensive? That's what's behind this particular order by Mr. Tole, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO did not have an offensive. It was called "Neretva 93." The HVO did not have any offensive, but wanted to prevent an offensive at that time. So I know of no offensive in that particular month and that it was linked to what Mr. Tole says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there's other documents that, if we had time, and perhaps someday we'll get to -- concerning what Mr. Praljak was doing around that time. Sir, can you also go to P11199, and we can also look at slide number 45. This is an order from Blaskic to the Kiseljak Brigade, 22 April 1993, and Mr. Blaskic gives specific guidance to his commander. Number 1: "If you can implement the task as a response to the provocations, but then do it in the most efficient way possible, accompanied with sending of reports and letters of protest regarding ABiH behaviour." Number 2: "Take the most favourable possible and always justify my orders as a response to provocations of the other side." And that was just sort of standard party-line behaviour, wasn't it? I mean, always say, We were only reacting to provocations, we were only, you know, defending ourselves. I mean, that was just kind of the standard language that commanders were basically taught or ordered, such as by Mr. Blaskic; that's how documents and reports and orders should be couched or postured, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said during my testimony that there was exaggeration in reports and that sometimes some things would be added on both sides, let me add.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record, the document we're discussing, it wasn't released on e-court, so we can't see what document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll certainly try to correct that, Your Honour, if it's not. It should also be in the binder. And if that's not the case, then -- if it's not on e-court, we will certainly correct that, Your Honours. But I think for the meantime, it is in the binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move forward to slide number 48. This is an excerpt from Mr. Prlic's, perhaps we'll call it, suspect interview which has been admitted in this case as P09078. This is what Mr. Prlic has said about HVO crime: "... in referring to the HVO, the war was fought by political leaders through the Main Staff of the HVO, actually through the military organs." That's at page 85 of the English transcript: "Now, who committed the crimes? It is quite clear that HVO military units, members of military units, committed the crimes, and therefore military authorities were responsible." English transcript page 74: "So as I said, I said that the soldiers, members of military units, were the ones who committed the crimes, or actually actions which could be described as war crimes, and therefore military authorities should be responsible, should be answerable for that ..." Transcript page 82-83. Can you tell us, sir, what is your reaction to Mr. Prlic's assessment and assertion that it was the HVO military, the military that you were in command of as either number 1 or number 2, was responsible for the crimes committed in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could interpret this in a different way. If he says it was politics via this, I don't see why it should be the political leaders that should be held responsible, because first of all he says that it was the political leaders, through the Main Staff. So I don't know what it is that Mr. Prlic was ultimately saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which political leaders do you say are responsible?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have, as political leaders, the entire Presidency, the government, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You know full well that various individual members of the HZ-HB Presidency were not pulling the levers of power. You identified for us last week, and you said, On the civilian side, the political leaders that had the most to do with the military and defence matters were Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic. And if you're going to start talking about the political leaders responsible for these matters, that's who you're talking about, isn't it; Mr. Boban, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They headed the structures. I mentioned the entire structures, the entire bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back, though, to Mr. Prlic's statement. And I disagree with you, respectfully, that you said, Well, it could be read differently. I put it to you, sir, that the second and third excerpts here cannot be read differently: "It is quite clear that HVO military units, members of military units, committed the crimes, and therefore military authorities," and I think it's fair to read at least in part, Your Honour -- Mr. Petkovic, "military authorities" read Slobodan Praljak and Milivoj Petkovic, "were responsible." The second -- the third excerpt, at the end: "... and therefore military authors," read Slobodan Praljak and Milivoj Petkovic, "should be responsible, should be answerable for that ..." So what do you say to Mr. Prlic about your responsibility for the crimes committed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not answer anything, but I would put the question: Who, then, should initiate the responsibility for the military authorities? The military authorities would not process themselves. Somebody must initiate the proceedings against the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, sir, did anyone in the HVO Herceg-Bosna power structures ever do that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were initiation of proceedings, and a large number of people were processed, especially in the major operation of 1994 when a large number of members of the HVO were processed, detained, criminal charges were pressed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, not for war crimes against Muslims, I'm going to represent to you, sir. And we'll come to that, hopefully, between now and the end of my examination. But you -- I want to -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to pick up on your answer just now, because you basically sort of, if I can put it this way, threw down the gauntlet, and you said, Well, if, in fact, the military authorities, Mr. Praljak, and I and others were responsible, then someone should have started -- instituted proceedings against us. But nobody did, did they, sir? Mr. Boban didn't, Mr. Stojic didn't, Mr. Prlic didn't. No one attempted to hold you responsible, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibility was established of others. Why should it be mine and Praljak's? We have shown you here a list of people whose responsibility has been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Ahmici as one example, because it's one that we know, from your prior statements, there's no dispute. You admit that Ahmici was a crime, you admit that Ahmici was committed by the -- crimes were committed by the HVO, you agree that the HVO units involved was the HVO military police, and you also agree, sir, don't you, that not a single HVO officer or soldier was ever prosecuted or punished for Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that. And in the Kordic case, I said that the Ahmici case was settled in the relationship between Mr. Boban and Mr. Blaskic, so Mr. Boban took the whole case into his own hands and he solved it with the commander of the operative zone. And you have two documents to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did he solve it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, he never informed the Main Staff or anyone else in the HVO. The correspondence between the two of them ended in the way they had agreed at their meeting in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've said before, and nothing you've said just now -- the reality is not a single HVO officer or soldier was ever prosecuted or punished in any way regarding Ahmici. That was true in 1993, and it's still true today, isn't it, by the HVO or Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what I stated, and I don't know why it wasn't. If Mr. Boban took things into his own hands, why did he conclude the Ahmici case in that way? I have no information that anyone was punished or held responsible for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you your knowledge goes farther than that. You know full well, and you've given the account before, that you specifically discussed these matters with Mr. Boban. And Mr. Boban was not going to prosecute anyone for Ahmici because he felt that the Muslim side was prosecuting people on their side, so, By gosh, we're not going to prosecute any HVO members either. That's what you were told, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his position, but he concluded the Ahmici case sometime in November, as far as I can remember, on the basis of the documents and the correspondence between him and Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you keep saying "he concluded," but you continue to confirm -- you affirm two things. Ahmici, he says -- or not prosecute anyone, I will not, we will not because I'm not going to do it if the Muslims aren't doing it. And, number 2, you confirm that no one was ever prosecuted or punished -- no HVO officer or soldier was ever punished. So I don't know why you keep saying it was concluded by Mr. Boban, as if it was a mystery. We know exactly that it wasn't concluded. No one was ever prosecuted; correct? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that no one was prosecuted, but in the document which is the correspondence between Blaskic and Boban, it was stated the Ahmici case has been completed according to your instructions. And I can't say anything more than that. None of us know what the instructions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, maybe the instructions were, at least, in part this, if that's the road you're going to take us down, sir. In fact, what happened, sir, beyond this is that people like Pasko Ljubicic and other suspected perpetrators of the Ahmici crimes were sent to Croatia and protected in Croatia for many years, until some of them began to come into either international or national jurisdictional custody, such as Mr. Pasko Ljubicic, who was originally was here at the Tribunal for some time, his case was transferred to the State Court in Sarajevo, and he pled guilty to Ahmici. But that was only years after hiding and being protected by the Croatian authorities; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he came to Croatia, but in 1993, when this correspondence took place between Boban and Blaskic regarding the Ahmici case, Pasko Ljubicic, still in 1994 - I'm not sure whether in 1995 as well - he was still in the HVO. When exactly he went to Croatia, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you remind me. Not only was Mr. Pasko Ljubicic at that particular time still in the HVO, he had been promoted after Ahmici. Not only was he not punished, he was promoted to more senior positions long after Ahmici, and when you and others knew full well that he was the responsible person. He was promoted, wasn't he? He moved from Central Bosnia to Mostar and was given a more senior position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what position he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know -- let's not hide. Let's not hide in technicalities, sir. I'm not going to ask you to give us the exact title, but you know full well that Mr. Ljubicic was moved -- was transferred to the Mostar region and was given a more senior position in the Herceg-Bosna HVO authorities, and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what position he was given. I know what position he had at the end of 1993. Whether that was more senior or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which position was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993, he was assistant chief for the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Now, what higher position he could have been given, I really don't know, and when he got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Don't you know, sir, that he subsequently received a higher position either in the military police or in the Ministry of Interior of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when. Tell me the year, and then -- I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've come quite close, but I still believe I have a bit of time, and I'm not going to be able to finish in the next five minutes. And I'm somewhat changing topics, so if I can please suggest that we stop there, and I will obviously finish early tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite, very well. Tomorrow morning, you will continue. Ms. Alaburic, how much time have you planned for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague Scott hasn't completed yet, so I can't give you a final estimate of the time I will need for my re-examination on the basis of his cross-examination. But according to my assessment now, roughly five hours would be quite sufficient for a re-examination for all the cross-examination and the Judges' questions. That is my estimate at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Scott has another 20 minutes tomorrow. If you need five hours, that is going to spill over onto Thursday. And 5D has been planned for 30 minutes, 4D for 15 minutes, that is, the witnesses for Thursday, the Prosecutor one hour, and the other Defences 30 minutes. That is the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we could manage to fit that in if there are no major interventions, that is, for me to complete my re-examination in the time I have planned. But what I can promise is that I'll do my utmost to make it as brief as possible, and I'll make some comparative checks of documents to be more efficient. So I think we could continue on Thursday with witnesses for the Defence of Mr. Coric, as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will intimate, with the leave of the Court, that there will be an application on behalf of Bruno Stojic for an additional half an hour for further cross-examination. The basis of this is that my learned friend Mr. Scott's cross-examination, of course, raised issues that had not been raised by -- in examination-in-chief. This is quite obvious from the transcript. If one refers, just by way of one example, to page 64 of the transcript, we will see a very clear attempt by the Prosecution to implicate Mr. Stojic in the running of prisons, and it was very clear that responsibility was being pushed in that direction. Now, when my learned friend Ms. Alaburic conducted her examination-in-chief, Your Honours will, of course, recall that there was no mention at all about the responsibility for the prisons and what happened therein. Your Honours, it's only right and fair that when the Prosecution seek to elicit evidence that is contrary to the interests of our client, we have a chance to test that evidence and contradict it, and that we will seek to do. It is our respectful submission that the half an hour requested is fair, is proportionate, and, indeed, is very modest when one looks at the time given to other parties in this matter. So, Your Honours, this is our application. You are seized of it, and we will raise it at the appropriate time again, should it be needed. However, I would ask Your Honours to consider this matter and perhaps come back with an additional ruling -- or with a ruling on this, unless further submissions are needed or additional clarification required by Bruno Stojic's team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I add, if that is important, that is, the position of General Petkovic's Defence with regard to this request, we consider this request to be completely well-founded, that it should be allowed, and that the colleagues should be allowed to have a re-cross regarding the issue raised in the cross-examination of the Prosecution. Let me remind you of two points. General Petkovic's Defence felt that it is not possible to use the witnesses of one Defence to build a case against another accused, and generally the Defence counsel should have enough time to protect the interests of their clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one additional point, with your leave, and I should have clarified it so there not be any doubt. The additional half an hour that we're seeking will come out of the time that the Stojic team has kept in reserve for this purpose, so we're not asking for additional time. We're simply asking to use the time that we kept in reserve for these kind of eventualities. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. For Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I just wish to ask, since we have certain obligations towards the Witness Protection Service, we have been changing the timetable so many times - we all know that - I would ask to know, as early as possible tomorrow, what the ruling of the Chamber is so we can inform the witnesses who have been planned for Thursday. Purely for these technical obligations, could we be informed as soon as possible so that we can do the necessary scheduling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will convey our decision. But, in any event, the witnesses for Thursday should be ready to enter the courtroom at 9.00. That's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
